Besides arable and garden cultivation and livestock breeding, industry is of great importance. Apart from the city of Zurich (see this article), for example, we find mechanical engineering in Oerlikon, Albisrieden, Altstetten, Schlieren; a wagon factory in Schlieren, cotton industry in Dietikon, etc.

The large railway junction Zurich dominates the traffic lines of the district. According to the natural terrain shape, we have the two lakeside railways along the lake, which mediate traffic with Chur and with the Arlberg; then the line to Baden, which leads to western Switzerland and Basel. A branch line goes to Affoltern-Zug. Through the northern ridge run, in a common tunnel, the lines to Schaffhausen, Romanshorn and St. Gallen and into the Glatt valley. Secondary lines are the Sihl Valley Railway, the Limmat Valley tramway with branch to Weiningen, the tram lines Zurich-Hoengg, Zurich-Oerlikon-Seebach, and the adhesion railway to the Uetliberg.
District Zurich.
Zurich (Canton and District Zurich).
1. Location and Extension.

Municipality and capital of the canton and district of Zurich, largest city of Switzerland. The geographical coordinates of the federal observatory on the Zurichberg (according to a kind communication from the observatory) are: 47° 22' 38" N latitude and 8° 33' 3.9" E longitude from Greenwich. The magnetic declination in 1908 was 11½° W. The altitude is 470 m for the observatory, and for the lake level an average of 408.6 m. The Limmat descends to level 400 m (before Hoengg) over a distance of 6 km within the city area, i.e. an average gradient of 1.5‰. The city area extends westward to the ridge of the Uetliberg, whose summit signal lies on the city boundary at 874 m above sea level.

To the south, the boundary follows the ridge to the Baldern, then descends including the former municipality of Leimbach to the Sihl and south of the Etlisberg between Wollishofen and Mönchhof to the lake. On the right bank, it runs south of the Burghölzli psychiatric hospital up to the Realp, crosses the Wehrenbach, follows the middle course of the Elefantenbach for a short distance, encircles the Loorenkopf, and from there in a fairly regular direction from SE to NW on the Glatt valley side of the Zurichberg and reaches the northern slope of the Käferberg via the saddle of the Milchbuck.

At Hardturm it touches the Limmat, which forms the municipal boundary up to below the Hoengger bridge. From there, irregular ditches in the wide Limmat valley are used as boundaries. The Triemli is circumvented to the southeast. From the Döltschi, the line rises again at the Uto and encloses, following its eastern ramp, northeast past the Hotel Uetliberg to the summit signal. Thus, the area of the city of Zurich united with its outer municipalities forms a horseshoe shape on the map around the lower lake basin and rises with both edges to the summit heights of the Uetliberg in the west, the Zurichberg, and Käferberg in the east. The area is 44.17 km^2.

The city area consists of the actual former Zurich in the center and a wreath of outer municipalities which have been united with the old town since 1893, namely: Wollishofen, Enge, Wiedikon, Aussersihl, Wipkingen, Unterstrass, Oberstrass, Fluntern, Hottingen, Hirslanden, and Riesbach. Thus, Zurich is the largest community in Switzerland.

Whoever visits Zurich for the first time should approach the city slowly by ship downstream on a mild summer evening. Lovely shores with decent villages accompany him on the left and right. Rich country houses thrust their oriels and turrets out of well-maintained gardens. The green pastures with the elongated evening shadows of the fruit trees on the left bank, the earthy, vitriol blue-spotted vineyards on the right bank become thinner and thinner. Residences succeed each other. We pass the bushy Zurichhorn, where the Hornbach has formed a wide, densely settled delta in the lake. The lake becomes narrower. On both sides, artificially reclaimed settlement areas stretch out. Above them rise on the left the venerable Belvoirpark and the rich villa quarters on the moraine hills of Enge; on the right the Zurichberg, a single airy garden city from the Hirslanderberg down to the Rigiquartier.
Zurich as seen from the lake.

The lake still gleams. Black-blue dark mixed forest, interspersed with dark yews, rises beyond the Sihl to the straight Uetliberg ridge, whose bare sandstone emerges here and there in hollow niches. Comfortable inns greet from the summit. The last golden rays of the evening sun flee up over the Zurichberg. Sharp-profiled the two Grossmünster towers, the slender Fraumünster spire and the Viennese delicate new Tonhalle block the way.

On the left are the Red and White Castles, the Rentenanstalt and "Unfall Zürich", on the right the city theatre and Uto castle, all built on former lake ground as if the old pile dwellings had risen again. In the depths the Limmat flows under the arches of the monumental Quaibrücke, and the St. Peter's tower with the large clock completes the characteristic silhouette symbolically as a sign of time. The joyful splashing of the baths gradually dies down. One light after another appears up the mountain slope in the jumble of houses. Evening star and spotlights from the Uto and the original Urania tower, or from the Tonhalle, squint at each other over the city, and as if by magic, a dazzling diadem lies on the forehead of the picture at the lakeside edge: banks and bridges have donned their light wreaths, so that the city is a beacon to the land even at night.

Thus, the picture gathers from both lake shores. As the lake is the outlet of the river, so is the human settlement concentrated at this point, where a ring of low glacial debris hills had to dam water and traffic.

The location for a larger settlement is thus given by nature: over the lake upwards and down the valley, traffic was facilitated by water; the lake itself, which can easily be blocked at the outlet, served simultaneously as a defense, and the moraine ridge was used to form an inner line of defense, while the higher mountains east and west form outer protective walls.

Once a settlement existed here, it had to become the destination for trade routes leading over the central and eastern Swiss Alps, while northern traffic routes from the Rhine merged here: Zurich became the depot for goods mediation between Italy and Germany. Its own industry, developed early, expansively made use of this favorable situation. It is indicative that the first Swiss railway ran from Zurich.

This "Spanish Brötli Bahn" to Baden was soon followed by other main lines. Today, Zurich is the hub of railway lines from Schaffhausen, from Winterthur and thereby from Romanshorn-Frauenfeld, Singen-Etzwilen and St. Gallen, from the Glatt valley, from the right and left lake shores (traffic from the Glarus region and from the canton of Graubünden, from the Arlberg, as well as Wädenswil-Einsiedeln and soon Ricken-Toggenburg), from Lucerne-Zug (Gotthard) and from Basel-Brugg and western Switzerland-Aarau-Brugg; not to mention numerous more local lines and ferry connections by steamship. All this has contributed to the present high significance of our largest Swiss city, one factor conditioning or promoting the other, like electricity and magnetism in the mechanism of a modern power machine.
2. Topographical Description.
Historical map of the city of Zurich

In the city map or the view from the heights of the Uetliberg, the hilly, angular old town with its dark, age-gray sandstone houses and blackened tile ridges distinctly separates from the wide-meshed, regulated street grid of the outer zone, whose blocks gradually dissolve uphill on both sides of the lake and Limmat into healthy villa quarters with open development. The angular shape of the Schanzengraben still betrays the extent of the former "small city" on the left Limmat bank, while Seilergraben-Hirschengraben enclose the "large" (right bank) city uphill. Within this old fortress framework, we want to begin our walk through the city. A ship took us to the landing stage at Bürkliplatz, formerly called Stadthausplatz. What beautiful parks lie to the left towards Enge and before us towards Bahnhofstrasse! We cross the Quaibrücke. Built in 1882/83 from coarse Black Forest granite, it bridges the Limmat's outflow from the lake with a length of 165 m.

From here, in clear, especially föhn weather, one enjoys a magnificent view of lake and mountains. To the left, behind the pointed church tower of Zollikon, rises the magnificent layered mass of the Glärnisch with the Vrenelisgärtli and the Bächistock behind the great firn shoulder. To the right follows the limestone block of the Faulen, in the front scene the obliquely striped Drusberg in the upper Sihl valley, then Bifertenstock, Tödi, Klariden, Scheerhorn, the elegant firn pyramid of the Düssistock; in the mid-ground, often standing out in dark blue-gray, the Mythen, further right behind the mighty Windgällen wall with the porphyry summit of the Kleinen Windgälle below to the right, and over the gap of Kaiserstock and Rossberg rising the ridge-rich Bristenstock.

The firn wreath extends to the western Urnäsch (Urirotstock, Schlossstock, and Wissig), before which the wooded molasse mountains of the Hohen Ronen and Gottschalkenberg and the Sihlwald on the Albis slope, as well as the low moraine ridge of the Zimmerberg up towards Hütten and Schindellegi, appear spread out like a green carpet, speckled lakewards with sunlit villages. Elegant church towers rise next to schools, and along the lake, numerous factory chimneys testify to rich industrial activity. Steam locomotives smoke on both shores, and small steamboats hustle busily back and forth, drawing garland lines along the shores: an unforgettable, incomparably beautiful picture, mixed from majestic alpine tranquility, lovely rural life, and bustling traffic—separated and yet connected by the wide blue lake surface.

Let us turn from the Quaibrücke downstream of the old town toward the Limmat. Across the former ferry landing square, now widened into a splendid quay, we reach the 1885 built Zwingli monument, a high bronze statue of the great reformer, framed by dark groups of trees, in front of the old Wasserkirche, in which the city library is now housed. To the north, the Helmhaus adjoins. From the Münsterbrücke offers a characteristic city view: to the right, elevated, the Grossmünster with its two Gothic towers—formerly ending in pointed spires, now crowned with wooden domes. It is the church of the former collegiate chapter, the place of Zwingli’s activity 1519–1531, built in Romanesque style in 1078 on the site of an older burnt church. On the southern tower, high up in a niche, sits, carved in stone, Emperor Charlemagne with the sword on his knees and a golden crown on his head. In the noteworthy cloister (upper daughters' school) stands a fountain with the statue of the emperor in sandstone.

Down the Limmatquai, some guild houses follow, then the venerable town hall, built over the Limmat. It is the third building on this site. The first was entirely wooden, the large (1400) at least toward the small (left bank) city wooden until 1502; in 1504 it received glass windows, previously only covered with cloth, and was demolished in 1694. Today's building is in noble German renaissance style. In the vestibule is a bust of the poet and Zurich state scribe Gottfried Keller. On the upper floor is the cantonal council chamber, also used as the session room by the great city council.
Zurich: Utoquai.

“The tribune for the listeners is well arranged,” wrote Meyer von Knonau in 1846, “but it would be somewhat cramped if always important matters were discussed and speakers of the first rank appeared.” From the town hall, the wide Gemüsebrücke with its blue-shaded market stalls leads the eye across to the green hill of Lindenhof with the Freemason lodge and the tower of St. Peter's Church with the mighty clock faces (until about the mid-16th century the only public clock in Zurich), down over the narrow-windowed, narrow and tall houses of the Schipfe and back at the Wühre past the richly Baroque-built guild house “zur Meise,” which represents bourgeois nobility in sandstone with its wrought-iron courtyard gate. Upward on the left bank follows the slenderly turreted Fraumünster church, founded by Ludwig the German in 853, with Hans Waldmann's tomb. Attached to it and tastefully connected with the old cloister (architect Gull) is the friendly town hall, the central office of municipal administration, and the federal post office. All these buildings are constructed from molasse sandstone from the Bäch and Bollingen quarries, whose dark weathering color gives the otherwise lovely cityscape a slightly melancholic touch. Comfortingly towering above the narrower cityscape is the new Prediger tower and the simple basilica of the Roman Catholic Liebfrauenkirche with its bluntly squared campanile of dazzling white tuff limestone. The Limmat is framed by the industrial buildings on piles of the two mill piers, and an almost comical note is added by the Urania tower with a cupola, which extends into a round gallery, housing the public observatory tower.

The Münsterbrücke, from which we gained this view of the old town, was inaugurated in 1838. It spans the river with four gently arched arches. “The vaults and cladding are made of black marble from the Wallenstadtsee quarries, the main cornice from white-bleached Gotthard granite, taken near Mellingen from massive erratic blocks lying there... This beautiful building was commissioned by the Zurich merchants under the direction of engineer Negrelli, constructed by Konrad Stadler and two other Zurich architects."
Zurich: Lower Limmatquai.

We follow the quay past the cheerful swan colony and “under the arches” to the town hall, then climb opposite the Fleischhalle and Gemüsebrücke up the Marktgasse. It is incomprehensible that this narrow passage once had to be the main traffic channel through which posts from eastern Switzerland rolled towards western Switzerland via Zurich. Soon we turn left, past the tall guild house zur Schmieden and the Rindermarkt to the Stüssihofstatt. There it looks medieval: narrow, angular alleys, sloping squares. Knight Stüssi gravely surveys the narrow area from the fountain. Through the hustle and bustle of the Niederdorf, throwing furtive glances into shady side alleys, we reach Leonhardplatz and the Bahnhofbrücke. Here is heavy traffic. Several tram lines converge here, and the bridge can hardly handle the flow of vehicles and pedestrians at times.

In the angle between the Limmat and Sihl lies the main station built as a terminal station, a pretty complex of the former Northeastern Railway Company, with allegorical figures above the middle building representing art, science, commerce, and industry. The spacious passenger hall long counted as one of the largest and most beautiful in the world, and the sumptuous waiting rooms were especially highlighted by travel guides. Today, these have been architecturally surpassed, but tight order and cleanliness in Zurich station, especially on busy holidays, impress.
Zurich: Bahnhofplatz towards the Polytechnic.

In the plaza promenade behind the station stands the Swiss National Museum, built by the city of Zurich from 1892–98 according to plans by architect Gull, an excellent example of the integration of architecture (medieval style) with the complex requirements of the individual museum departments. Especially famous are Ferdinand Keller's pile dwelling finds previously kept in the Helmhaus and the weapons hall with Hodler's mural (Swiss retreat from the battle of Marignano).

Further, numerous original rooms, including three Gothic ones from the Fraumünster Abbey Zurich from 1489 and 1507, the treasury with coin cabinet in the basement, a large porcelain collection, etc. The National Museum was founded in 1891 by the Confederation and solemnly inaugurated on June 25, 1898. In the lovely layouts before the confluence of the Limmat and Sihl, simple monuments to the Minnesinger Hadlaub, the idyll poet Gessner, and Wilhelm Baumgartner, the creator of the incomparable singing style for Gottfried Keller’s "Oh my homeland," delight us.

In front of the station, we admire the large monumental fountain of red granite with the statue of Alfred Escher by Richard Kisling, erected in place of a tall fountain in 1889, and now turn to Bahnhofstrasse. What a contrast to the narrow, high-gabled alleys of the right bank! Its lime tree avenue spreads out with beneficial breadth, twice bending left at a blunt angle towards Paradeplatz and to the lake. It skirts the moraine hill quarter of Oetenbach (formerly prison buildings, built from the remains of the old Oetenbach monastery, now demolished and artificially cut through at Uraniastrasse), Rennweg, Lindenhof, Strohhof and leaves the isolated glacial debris hills of St. Anna and the Katz (botanical garden) on the right. It begins with beautiful hotel buildings in French architecture at the station; it follows the Linth Escher school in a pretty park setting; in front the Pestalozzi memorial. Then large-scale, modern shops and department stores, window display after window display, at the top the large blocks of the central and Kappelerhof and the stock exchange built by the Zurich trade society from 1877–80. Noteworthy are also the buildings of the large banking institutions: Swiss Bank Association and Swiss Credit Institution at Paradeplatz, Bank Leu and Zurich Cantonal Bank, as well as the federal bank and Swiss People's Bank on Bahnhofstrasse, some with richly furnished vestibule rooms, especially the Swiss Bank Association (colossal statue symbolizing trade, by Richard Kisling). A look is still cast into the old, angular Augustinergasse with its cozy oriels.

Then the lake draws us again, and we walk out on the Alpenquai through splendid parklands, which were decided in 1881 and inaugurated in 1887. Pleasant perspectives open between bushes and groups of trees over well-kept lawns and rich flower beds. A cleverly assembled arboretum of native and exotic trees is spread over artificial hills and valleys. Erratic blocks of the old Linth glacier, red fieldstones from the Walensee area, Speer nail conglomerate, chalk and Jurassic limestones from Glärnisch alternate in colorful order, with gentians, alpine roses bushes and heathland herbs peeking out as if by chance.

The quay is essentially the work of quay engineer A. Bürkli, for whom a tasteful monument has been erected. The city is also indebted to geologist Albert Heim for ensuring through his efforts that the natural moraine character of the city topography is preserved even in this artificial landscape. A pretty background is formed by the new Tonhalle, the Zurich Trocadero, built by the Viennese architects Fellner and Helmer in 1895, the “Red Castle,” Palais Henneberg with marble frieze, the “White Castle” of Savonnières limestone and the building of the Swiss pension institution of colorful limestone. The public Belvoirpark, once the property of the Zurich statesman Alfred Escher, the champion of the Gotthard railway, makes the end. From his daughter Dr. Lydia Welti-Escher, the magnificent estate was bequeathed to the Confederation, later purchased by a society, and later largely handed over to the city as property.

From Belvoirpark, we ascend over the Gabler to Bürgli to the picturesque church of Enge, enjoy the lovely view over city and lake and the nearby expensive noble villa quarter of Enge, and then cross the outer moraine parallel ridge beyond Waffenplatzstrasse to the Sihl. Often it can be crossed almost dry-footed, but quite often it rolls meter-deep murky waves between Zimmerberg and Albiskette over the commons (the federal weapons place) of the city and its original bed, the present-day Limmat. At the Uto bridge, the path branches off to the Uetliberg, past the Albisgütli shooting house, where shooting festivals and the boys' shooting competition are held.

Then the surroundings come alive with a joyful, noisy fairground, crowds sway up and down like at the Theresienwiese at the Munich Oktoberfest. In old Albisgütli there used to be “donkeys and horses with guides” ready for visitors of the mountain before the Uetliberg railway was built. Several large brick and brickworks mark, lined up in front of large clay pits at the foot of the Uetliberg, the outskirts of the industrial city district, which we now want to get to know more closely.

Along the Sihl downstream, wedged between the Sihl and the Sihl canal, we reach the Sihlhölzli, the former shooting ground, now playground and ice skating rink. On the left above, the mighty Bühl schools and the pretty new church of Wiedikon dominate on quaint moraine hill remains. Rectangular barrack-like blocks are the signature of the districts Wiedikon and Aussersihl lying to the left of the Sihl. Here and there still a few old-fashioned low, cozy houses from village times, but overall cramped tenement houses, smoky, weathered, and tasteless.

We cross the left-bank lake railway, which reaches the main station in a wide arc west of Aussersihl, visit Stauffacher bridge and Sihl bridge, and gradually retreat via the busy Badenerstrasse past St. Jakob's church with 1400 seats and a large singers' podium (built in 1901) and several new school palaces, leaving the barracks area with arsenal on the right, towards Langstrasse. On Sundays there is a true pilgrimage of excursionists heading for the Zurichberg or Uetliberg, or just to stroll the streets.
Zurich: In the quay grounds.

The street is one of the longest in greater Zurich; it passes under the combined approach lines of the main station and leads over to Limmatplatz in the industrial district north of the railway. Nearby stand St. John’s church and several other large new school buildings. Industrial establishments of the greatest scale are in operation in this district on both sides of the long double viaduct, over which trains from Oerlikon and the right lake shore (from the Lettentunnel at Stadelhofen) rattle down the far-reaching curve to the lower station level.

Along the left Sihl bank (Sihlquai) the “industrial railway,” a goods line extending almost to the main station, ends there in a dead-end, conveying traffic to the large factories. We name the renowned machine factory Escher-Wyss & Co., the Steinfels soap factory, the joint-stock brewery, the city mill, etc. The municipal filter plants for drinking water are also located on the Sihlquai, and further downstream across the Limmat, pumping and power plants near Letten station. Past the former gasworks, now arranged for troop accommodation (cavalry) in case of mobilization, we reach outside the viaduct the newly widened Wipkinger bridge, with a pretty view downstream of the Limmat valley and to the village of Hoengg leaning gently against the slope of Käferberg. With the right Limmat bank, we enter the fourth city district, pass through Wipkingen, which still largely retains its village character, cross Röschibachstrasse and the kilometres-long Nordstrasse, go through Rotbuchstrasse up to Rötel. There is lively construction activity here, as almost everywhere on the city periphery. We have the choice to travel back by the Oerlikon-Seebacher tramway or with the newest “city” line through Weinbergstrasse through the district Unterstrass to Leonhardsplatz at the Bahnhofbrücke.
Zurich: Wiedikon, the church and the schools.

Or we continue the mountain walk to the magnificent school building on Riedlistrasse above the church and via newly laid out, significantly changing road routes, where everything is in the process of becoming and growing, up into the freely built, garden-rich Rigi quarter. On the Höhenstrasse we enjoy the magnificent overview of the city and surroundings. Those interested in statistics count about twenty churches plus less prominent minority chapels, the numerous new schoolhouse roofs and, down the valley, the busily smoking factory chimneys down to the three mighty gasometers of the city gasworks in Schlieren.

Now we best recognize the wonderful location of the city at the outlet of the large lake, at the confluence of the Limmat and Sihl, open valley upwards and valley downwards, capable of expansion, laterally limited by the almost straight Uetliberg ridge and the gently rolling Zurichberg: generously laid out in main lines, nourished and moved by the tame lake water and the wild young Sihl, and nicely limited on the sides by established, not excessively high rock walls. One almost wants to say that this Zurich natural picture resembles in miniature the character of the population and their institutions.

From the Höhenstrasse down, one overlooks the impressive building complex of the cantonal and federal universities. Above all, the main building of the Swiss Federal Polytechnic School deserves mention. The school was founded in 1855, includes the construction school, engineering school, mechanical, agricultural and forestry departments, a department for training specialized teachers in mathematics and natural sciences, a philosophical-economic (so-called free subjects) department, and a military science department.

The main building, built according to plans by Gottfried Semper from 1861–64 and fully operational since 1864, stands foremost on the scenic ramp of the university complex towards the old town. In the middle building, crowned by a series of allegorical figures by sculptor Graf, is a beautiful aula that has served both universities until now. Here and in the vestibule stand busts of school board president Dr. Kappeler (Hörbst) and professors Kopp and Bolley, as well as Semper and Culmann (Richard Kisling).

The northern facade is decorated with sgraffito. The south wing is currently occupied by the University, which will soon receive a magnificent new home in close proximity. Behind the polytechnic stands the old chemical laboratory (hygienic institute). A whole network of scientific institutes line up: federal materials testing institute, federal testing institute for fuels, federal machine laboratory (built 1899/1900), federal chemical laboratories (occupied 1886) with the Swiss agricultural chemical institute and seed control station, federal central office for forestry research, agricultural and forestry school (1874) with experimental garden, federal observatory, federal physics building (1890), with the Swiss meteorological central institute, cantonal hospital, laboratory of the cantonal chemist and dental polyclinic (1899/1900), anatomy, isolation hospital, pathological institute (1832), eye clinic, blind and deaf-mute institute, cantonal physics and physiology building, and recently (spring 1909) opened cantonal chemical laboratories of the University and new cantonal school building opposite the old cantonal school on Rämistrasse, built in 1839–42 by architect Wegmann. At that time, the cubic meter cost 13.5 francs; today, school buildings cost almost double! Adjacent to the city are the Wolfbach schoolhouse, the music conservatory in Florhofgasse (1900–1902) with large concert hall (450 seats), the magnificent Hirschengraben schoolhouse, and the collegiate building at Rechberg, an old, handsome patrician house.

Truly a blessed district of intellect, where canton and Confederation compete to build worthy places for science and the disciplines of its technical application! And one must not forget what the city itself does for its school system. See the chapter “Education” under “Zurich canton.” Especially striking in the cityscape are the municipal school buildings. At the time of the city unification in 1893, there were 39 schoolhouses in the old city and the outer municipalities combined, the oldest being the plain schoolhouse at Badenerstrasse (occupied 1821) and the youngest the tall school palace at Hirschengraben (1893, architect Alexander Koch). Since then, almost every year a school building (with gyms, bathing facilities, school kitchens, workshops, modeling rooms, small school gardens, etc.) has been added. In the new buildings, classrooms are planned for a maximum of 55 primary or 35 secondary students; with 7×10–11 or 7×9 meters floor space, low-pressure steam and hot water heating; air heating has been abandoned. The costs amounted to (1889-1902) per class 42,000 Fr., per student 770 Fr., per m3 25.73 Fr. (“pure construction costs”).

Through friendly villa quarters, our way finally leads from the Höhen- and Bergstrasse to the Dolder Forest House at the entrance to the large beautiful Dolderpark. We are near the highest edge of the inhabited city area and ride with the cable car past the mighty dome of the Kreuzkirche down to Römerhof and from there with the municipal tram past the original St. Antonius church through Hottingen via Kreuzplatz-Bahnhof Stadelhofen south of the tree-crowned hill of the High Promenade (Nägeli Monument, French and English churches) to the city theater (built by Fellner and Helmer in Vienna, inaugurated in autumn 1891; the old theater at Untern Zäune burned down on the night of January 1/2, 1890) and the Corso Theater (variety stage opened in 1900) and past the old Tonhalle square back to Quaibrücke, where we started the tour.

The short tour through the city could not touch many districts, as we got to know the inner old town and the younger outer zones in two concentric ellipses. Two pretty oases in the jumble of houses must, however, be specially added: first, the Heimplatz near Pfauen Theater (the city theater’s drama stage) with the monument to the singing father Ignaz Heim and the new art house, whose completion will crown years of efforts by enthusiasts of fine arts; nearby the upper court with the jury court chamber and the plain “Obmann office” (former Barefoot monastery), the central office of cantonal administration, with many branches housed in neighboring buildings due to lack of space.

And second, the botanical garden, laid out in 1836 on the former “Bollwerk zur Katze” in the west corner of Schanzengraben. It includes a morphological-biological plant section, a systematic department, tropical useful and ornamental plants in greenhouses, as well as phytogeographic groups (Alpinum). The museum houses a type herbarium for the identification of Swiss plants accessible to the public; it also holds an extensive herbarium of the canton of Zurich, a Helveticum herbarium and a general herbarium, along with some specialist herbaria (including those of Hegetschweiler and Gessner), as well as fruit and model collections. The park is adorned with monuments to botanists Heinrich Zollinger, Oswald Heer, A. de Candolle, and Konrad Gessner. Nearby in Selnau, near the Uetliberg and Sihl valley railway station, is the narrow district office, with a mighty erratic block in front.
Zurich: Badenerstrasse and Saint Jakob's Church.

Picturesque small-town, almost medieval is the physiognomy of the innermost city districts, in whose often unhygienic narrow alleys the native himself finds it difficult to find his way; note on the city map the small labyrinth around the Peter tower and up to the Gemüsebrücke, or on the right bank between the Limmat and Zäune-Neumarkt-Rindermarkt. Many houses still bear cheerful names according to old custom, often of historical significance: zur Windegg, Kerze, zum Loch, zum Pflug, Königsstuhl, Kropf, Wellenbaum, Einhorn, zum steinernen Erggel, das Gut zum Rechberg, der Beckenhof, der Strohhof, Friesenberg, etc. Original oriels decorate the fronts of Kirchgasse, Schipfe, lower Zäune, Augustinergasse, and heavy wrought iron grills are thoughtful door and window sculptures, bearing witness to tasteful solidity (Unicorn, Candle, Town Hall, Rechberg, Orphanage, Meise, etc.). Gradually, however, the old type disappears, although historically valuable objects are preserved by respectful restorations (paneling and wooden ceilings of the guild houses zur Schmieden, zur Saffran, Zimmerleuten, etc.). The cityscape must change over time.

Even today, the dark green-gray sandstone center of the city is distinctly separated from the outer districts, for whose construction whole sample cards of building materials were already available: white Dielsdorf Lägern limestones, so-called Solothurn marble, massive Black Forest granite from the Albthal; alpine chalk limestones and red Vosges sandstones for paving stones. Glimmer-rich Reuss protogine or Ticino gneiss, even delicately pink granite from Baveno (Italy) at Lake Langensee is brought by the Gotthard railway, and large quantities of easily workable Savonnières fossil limestone are imported from France. The farther one gets to the periphery, to the districts under development, the more varied, depending on the practical use, are the building stones and building style. Foreign material has already found its way into the old town, where modern business palaces are built instead of cozy bourgeois houses. At the Zwingli monument in front of the Wasserkirche, for example, 9 different types of rock were used for the worthy construction of the simple bronze statue. And yet even in the old city center, sandstone gradually displaced a formerly closer, colorful building material: the former moraine blocks, which still appear here and there in old masonry during demolition. Even in the 12th and 13th centuries, houses “were unsightly, mostly wooden huts, about two storeys high, with one room into which two, often three households shared, and several chambers. Stone houses were among the greatest rarities at the time, so they were explicitly named as such in documents... After the terrible fire of 1313 that consumed more than half of the small city, an ordinance was issued that every rebuilt house should at least have one floor masonry...” (Meyer von Knonau: Der Kanton Zürich. 1844. Vol. I, pp. 231 ff.). Still quicker disappeared the people whom these houses sheltered in joy and sorrow. Numerous marble memorial plaques respectfully remind us of famous names, whose historical glory often stands in strange contrast to the simple hut of the birth or death house or the place of former activity of the honored person: Zwingli's office apartment at Kirchgasse, Heinrich Pestalozzi’s birthplace at Rüdenplatz, birthplace of Gottfried Keller at Rindermarkt, house of Escher von der Linth at Sihlstrasse, and many others.

4. Population.

According to the results of the federal census of 1900, the city of Zurich then had 150,703 inhabitants. Of these, 30,891 or about 2/10 were citizens of the city, 30,864, almost exactly the same number, citizens of other municipalities in the canton, 45,187 or 3/10 citizens of other cantons, totaling 106,942 or 7/10 Swiss citizens, and 43,761 or 3/10 foreigners. The religious distribution was as follows: Protestants 102,794, Catholics 43,655, Israelites 2,713, others or unknown 1,541. By mother tongue: German 140,803, French 2,586, Italian 5,100, Romansh 415, other languages 1,799. 47.5% of the population was male and 52.5% female.
From earlier times, the literature gives the following population numbers for the city of Zurich:

After the city unification in 1893, the population increased rapidly. However, the economic downturn of 1899/1900 brought a period of decrease. Since 1902, the number has been rising again, albeit more slowly. The estimated population at the end of 1906 was 172,855; end of 1907: 177,437; end of 1908: 180,224. The actual number is probably 1,000 to 2,000 lower, due to traditionally incomplete deregistrations, especially of Italian migrant workers, whose return migration in the winter months usually represents a counter flow.
The residential population increased by 4,582 persons in 1907, i.e., by 2.65%. If the increase continues evenly, the number should reach about 200,000 around 1912 or 1913.

The following figures for 1907 give an orientation of population movement: Number of births: 4,921 (2,357 girls and 2,564 boys), deaths: 2,710 (1,323 female, 1,387 male), both including stillbirths (99 girls, 96 boys). Marriages: 1,674. Divorces: 212. Naturalizations: 1,397, of which 931 were free, 466 by purchase; of these naturalized, 829 came from the canton of Zurich, 129 from the rest of Switzerland, and 439 from abroad.

The marriage rate fell steadily between 1898 and 1903, from 1,816 to 1,417, a reduction of 22%; it has risen slightly since. Also, the surplus of births, still 2,702 in 1899, has been falling continuously since 1901; in 1905 it was only 1,919, despite the rising population. In 1901 the live birth rate was 32.84‰, in 1906 25.23‰, in 1907 23.25‰ of the mid-year population. Of course, mortality also declined but not as much as the birth rate. Increased cost of living results in reduced marriage opportunities. The socio-political development affects the small and middle classes in various ways. What else can be said if, in a largely commercial and industrial metropolis of 81,531 taxpayers in 1907, only 1,678 (including cantonal and municipal officials) declared an income of 5,100 Fr. and more, of whom only 1,026 such over 6,100 Fr. and only 298 such over 10,100 Fr., and only 1,532 taxpayers over 100,000 Fr. assets?
Zurich: Stadthausquai.
Within one year, the following mutation amounts arise in the resident population, corresponding to the normal year 1906 with an average annual population of 170,400:

Within the city about 78,000 persons moved (11,500 families). About 44,000 persons moved in, about 40,700 moved out. Gain of 3,300 persons. Marriages in the resident population: 1,750. Births about 4,300 persons. Deaths about 2,550 persons. Surplus of births: 1,750. Annual increase: 5,050. Guests staying in hotels about 300,000 persons.

Conspicuous is the high move rate. About 40% of the resident population moves once a year! Half of this number concerns family moves, not just individual moves, mostly at the beginning of April or October, but also at other quarter beginnings. (Cologne 44%, Breslau 49%; Dresden 28%, Nuremberg 36%). In the process, the old town in particular becomes deserted, which, as in most large German cities becoming the city center, is subject to “displacement of the indigenous population in language and custom.” District I had in 1895 = 29,500, end of 1900 = 25,900, and in 1906 still 20,000 inhabitants, the same as early as 1860! Immigration is considered to be those who stay more than two months; it amounted to 27,100 in 1893 and already 40,300 persons in 1905. These numbers are relatively high, although balanced by an almost equally high emigration rate.

The year 1908 showed a migration gain of only 913 persons with an immigration of 45,403 and an emigration of 44,490 (compared to 2,735 in 1907)—never so low since 1902. The economic depression is cited as the cause, which is expressed particularly in reduced immigration and multiple movements of Italians; compared to the previous year, Italian immigration fell from 8,200 to 7,100. Number of marriages 1,877 (maximum since 1893).

For the first time since 1901, the number of births increased, to 4,246 (birth rate per 1,000 inhabitants = 23.64); the number of deaths reached 2,372 (mortality rate per 1,000 inhabitants = 13.21). Birth surplus 1,874, making a total increase in the resident population of 2,787 persons or 1.57%. The migration gain included 536, the birth surplus 1,080 foreigners. The city-citizen population has been in significant decline for years due to excess deaths, and the marriage rate was, for example, proportionally always higher among the resident German Reich citizens than among the Zurichers themselves. Foreigners have predominated in the still remaining birth surplus in recent years, e.g., with 53.4% in 1907. If this continues, Zurich can soon exist without Zurichers; lucus a non lucendo!

Interesting is the immigration into the city according to the different source regions and their distance. Of the 40,289 immigrants in 1905, 21,711 were foreigners, half of whom were Germans, a quarter Italians, and a quarter from Austria, Russia, France, etc. 42.5% of all immigrants came directly from abroad to Zurich; of those coming from other Swiss locations, another 30% were foreigners. 16% of all immigrants were dependents, the rest 84% self-employed. More than 4/5 of all immigrants move for economic reasons. The closer the immigration occurs in kilometers, the greater it is, and the more dependents are relatively involved alongside self-employed. In 1905, 34.1% of all immigrants came from a distance of up to 50 kilometers (of which 1/4 came from at most 10 km), 19.5% came from 50–100 km distance, and so on—still a full 23.1% from over 300 km.
Zurich: Gemüsemarkt and St. Peter's Church.

The steady increase in population is not matched by an increase in housing opportunities. In the inner city, more and more former apartments are being converted into department stores and offices, and despite lively construction activity in the outer districts, which is often interrupted by strikes, it does not meet the steadily growing demand. As a result, rents have increased enormously in recent years. With an average room price of 279 Fr. (1906/07; since then even higher)—average including attic rooms—Zurich marches near the top of Swiss cities.

The city has already taken the right step to establish an official municipal housing register, which has been in operation since June 1906 and is suitable to provide guidance on the future development of construction by insight into the housing market. The city also builds its own apartment blocks. In 1907, a total of 213 new buildings were built with 696 apartments and insured for 17.4 million Fr. In 1907, Zurich counted 14,641 buildings. 750 of them have been added since 1899.

Since the general removal of the old ramparts and leveling of their ditches in 1833, the structural development of the city has thrived. Especially through the city unification in 1893, it took a tremendous upswing. The unexpected increase in population figures and general economic changes had great influence on construction activity. A new building law for localities with urban conditions (1893) requires greater distance of houses from neighboring plots (3.5 m). Previously, everyone built more or less for themselves as they liked. In 1770, houses were on average 2½ storeys high.

Then came high apartment houses. The new building law no longer allows the 6th residential floor and requires a minimum height of 2.5 m for living rooms. In 1901, regulations for open development of large districts were added. This seems to have paved the way for a return to single-family houses. Before 1900, such were only 7.6% of all residential buildings, afterwards already 19.8%. The system keeps land prices within reasonable limits. Around 1900, a reaction appeared in the form of a construction and real estate crisis.
Zurich: Paradeplatz.
Since 1809 there has been the state fire insurance with model registration of construction activity. Zurich today with its current territorial extent counted

The total insurance value of private buildings with and without apartments and public buildings was in 1906 681.9 million Swiss francs. Residential buildings relatively increase in the city compared to industrial buildings; the industry moves to the surrounding towns with cheaper land. Zurich thus becomes more a residential city again, except for the old town.
In 1906, there were a total of 35,900 apartments in the city.

5. Hygienic Conditions.

In earlier times, the natural water conditions of the lake, Limmat, and Sihl likely had a significant influence on the city’s health conditions. It is reported that, for example, in 1344 an inundation washed away the house “zum Schwert” and three mills, whose debris destroyed the bridge at Hardturm. In 1553, one could paddle around Fraumünster in a canoe, and in 1556, the Limmat flowed over the mill piers.

The Sihl also occasionally flooded the Platzspitz. In 1404 and 1512, however, one could walk dryfoot from Weinplatz, then called Kornhausplatz, to the town hall, and the big stone below the lower (vegetable) bridge was dry in 1580, 1585, 1654, 1740, and 1814. Today, water levels are so regulated that even extremely dry years, as the last ones including 1908, bring very low water levels but no further major disadvantages.

The average lake level is 409.2 m above sea level. The highest level reached was 411.00 m on July 8, 1817; the lowest 408.50 m on January 29, 1854; 408.56 m on February 25, 1882, and 408.60 m on February 25, 1891. Similar figures were brought recently in March 1909 (zero point of lake and Limmat gauges 411.28 m). Average discharge (Limmat and Schanzengraben) is 87 m³/s, with a maximum of 350 m³/s on June 15, 1876, and a minimum of 15.5 m³/s on February 25, 1891. (Lake area 87.78 km², water content 4,000 million m³, catchment area 1,819.7 km²).
Zurich: The Schipfe.

The lake acts health-conserving, besides as a general climatic factor, as a bathing opportunity (average surface temperature 10.9 °C; maximum 22.0 °C; at 16 m depth 5.9 or 11.6 °C). The city of Zurich maintains 11 public bathhouses in the lake, in the Limmat, and in the Schanzengraben, which register 300,000 to 400,000 visitors annually. Three of them are free. In 1907 (bad summer) 289,077 paying visitors were recorded, in 1906 343,816. Even in winter, individuals bathe in the lake (“polar bear club”), even during frozen lake conditions (winter swimming pools are missing; a related experiment was abandoned). The city also grants annual subsidies to the air and sun bath facilities of the nature cure association and recently expanded the men's bathhouse at Bürkliplatz for air baths.

As the lungs of the city, an impressive number of open spaces, parks, and promenades function. The old city already had its Lindenhof, the “historical core point of the city,” on which the Roman castrum Turicense and later a royal palace were said to have stood, the Winkelwies on the Geissberg, and the old shooting meadow, now Platzspitz promenade. Later came the botanical garden, Sihlhölzli, High Promenade, with old churchyard, Heimplatz, Stadelhoferplatz, town hall facilities, and the large quays with the wonderful quay facilities, which stretch like green foliage from Belvoirpark to the Quaibrücke and from there on the right bank to Zurichhorn, whose friendly old willows Rudolf Koller painted many beautiful motifs from. With respectful understanding, the city fathers tend our old trees. General dismay was felt when a large part of the facilities were damaged on May 24, 1908, by unusual snow load on the young leafy branches, and if a rotten poplar has to be felled or a beloved maple trunk sacrificed to traffic requirements, an outcry rises in all the city's papers.
Zurich: Zurichhorn.

Where new quarters arise, open spaces with trees and playgrounds are provided: Limmatplatz, Rotwand area, etc. Tennis courts are laid out in various places, and in winter, skating and toboggan opportunities are found.

The area of municipal facilities already amounts to over 320,000 m² today, and there are 4,000 street trees in the city alleys (1905). In addition, there are several hotel parks (Baur au Lac, Dolder), many front gardens of new houses, and villa-rich districts with open development on the slopes of the Zurichberg and at the Uetliberg foot. But the most beautiful are the large forest promenade facilities on the Zurichberg, Käferberg, and Uetliberg itself, which the Beautification Association of Zurich and Surroundings has laid out since its foundation in the early 1870s.

Honor such tireless charitable work! Thousands stroll here on Sundays in these green halls, enjoy the numerous benches of beautiful quiet nature and the winding underbrush paths with their artistic bridges and exquisite surprises (Manessebrünneli at Uetliberg, Waldhüsli, Elephant, Grandmother Beech, Battle Memorial [1799], Waterfall in Sagentobel, Stöckentobel, at Wehrenbach and on the Weidberg). And the Uto peak with its observation tower can become a true popular assembly when winter fog lies over the valleys, but the ridge ramps up into sunny warmth, or when the sun “jumps” on Ascension morning.

As far as the Black Forest and Vosges go, the view reaches beyond and far over the silver bands of the Aare loops into the Jura ridges, north towards the old Hegau volcanic cones of Hoherstoffel and Hohentwiel, and from the Alps the Uetliberg offers the most distinguished overview from Säntis to the Bernese Oberland ice giants. Neatly laid out like a gigantic toy spread out at the feet from Spelterini’s balloon perspective are the thoroughly interwoven jumble of houses of the city and the blue lake with its busy steam swallows, Sunday rowers, elegant sailboats and sports sculls; further up, the friendly lakeside villages and the wooded Sihl valley with the large city forest Sihlwald and the municipal game park.

The street cleaning and removal system can be satisfactory in Zurich. Compared to other larger cities, the city stands out advantageously. In summer, spraying cars with a range of 5 and 7.5 m, partially connected to the electric tram operation, take care to suppress dust; on sidewalks with hand carts. The previously used steam hose was largely abandoned because it was expensive and obstructive to traffic. Cleaning is done with sweeping rollers. Rapid snow removal (emptying into the Limmat) from main streets in winter, where unemployed people find welcome employment. There is a municipal garbage incineration plant (garbage collected in 1907: 58,390 m³ equal to 21,293 t, of which 20,231 t were incinerated) and a carcass burning facility (Podewils system). Excretions are collected in buckets; in 1907: 7,848 m³ in 10,441 buckets with 218,502 exchanges; bucket washing at the Hardhüsligut. There are 64 sanitary facilities in the city in total (oil urinals, Beetz system). Residential conditions were reported in the “Population” section.
Zurich: House zum Rüden.

Food and food control. The official meat inspection provides reliable data on meat consumption. There had so far been three public and 35 private slaughterhouses and a central meat hall for sale, besides numerous private sales outlets. A large municipal slaughterhouse will be completed in 1909. Cost about 6 million francs. In 1907, the following were slaughtered: 3,338 breeding oxen, 6,820 oxen, 1,675 cows, 2,611 cattle, 23,519 calves, 29,640 pigs, 5,547 sheep, 228 goats, 307 horses, and 98 rabbits, with a total weight of 7,687,787 kg. In addition, imports of meat (including poultry and fish) of 3,954,903 kg, totaling 11,642,690 kg; corresponding to a daily meat consumption of 173 g per head of population (1906: 169 g). The meat prices per half kilo were: breeding bull meat 85–90 cts. (1906: 80–85 cts.), ox and beef 75–95 (80–95), cow meat 55–75 (65–75), veal 100–125 (110–120), pork 90–115 (110–115), mutton 80–100 (70–90), horse meat 40 (40) cts. More than three quarters of slaughtered meat came from Switzerland, and barely one quarter was foreign cattle.

In 1907, 119,700 liters of milk were imported daily, at a selling price of 23 cents. On average, there were 5.4 controls per seller in the year. Negotiations on milk supply are ongoing between the city and the cooperative food association. Until now there have been particularly two large dairies on a private basis.

An original legacy from earlier times is the market with vegetables, fruits, and other foodstuffs held twice weekly on the open street throughout the year, Tuesdays and Fridays. Until 11 a.m. on these days, the sidewalks of certain centrally located streets are crowded with market stalls and cheerfully bargaining people: Bahnhofstrasse, Petersstrasse, Münzplatz, Uraniastrasse, Sihlhofstrasse, Usteristrasse, Schweizergasse, Lintheschergasse, Schützengasse, Rathausquai (under the arches), Rathausbrücke, Hirschengraben, Stauffacherstrasse.

The domestic products market on Bahnhofstrasse and its side streets regularly had 727 vendors in 1907, often over 1,200 in the autumn. Of these, 75% were self-producers. Depending on the type of food, a certain though not too strictly enforced separation in different street districts is recognizable. The flower market is always the most beautiful at the upper end of Bahnhofstrasse. In autumn, from mid-September to mid-November, there is a wholesale market for fruit and potatoes at Uraniastrasse and Hirschengraben. In 1907, the following quantities were imported: 3,000 q of apples at 16 to 48 Fr., few pears (30–40 Fr. per q), 120 q of plums at 11–13 Fr., and 316 q of potatoes at 7–8 Fr. The fruit mainly came from the districts of Zurich, Bülach, Dielsdorf, Horgen, and Uster and from the cantons of Aargau and Zug; plums also from Alsace; potatoes from Rafzerfeld and the canton of Schaffhausen. Around Christmas, Hirschengraben and many other city squares come alive with a cheerful Christmas tree market. In 1907, about 1,700 fir trees were sold.

At the end of 1907, Zurich had 1,061 inns (including 85 hotels) and about 1,000 small retail outlets for spirits. According to the rightly existing liquor law, 174 are too many in relation to the (updated) population of the city. While there is one inn per 131 inhabitants in the entire canton, certain districts of the city of Zurich have a worrying excess. For example, in the Niederdorf there are 29 pubs on 74 houses, at Zeughausstrasse 10 on 23 houses, at Seebahnstrasse 11 on 45, Konradstrasse 11 on 46, Zwinglistrasse 10 on 34, Langstrasse 28 on 91 houses.

A salutary influence is exerted by the 28 temperance and coffee houses, which enjoy an ever-increasing frequency. In the 9 alcohol-free establishments of the Women’s Association for Temperance and Public Welfare, 7,000 to 8,000 guests visit daily; 260 female employees find employment and housing here. The association's businesses began 12 years ago, growing steadily from modest beginnings; today they have annual assets and liabilities exceeding one million francs.

Despite or perhaps because of the minimal retail profits, everything rests on a solid, calculated basis of self-sufficiency. Rapid amortization can take place, and the three large public houses “Zurichberg,” “zum blauen Seidenhof,” and “zum Olivenbaum,” each valued at about half a million, as well as the newly expanded restaurant “Karl dem Grossen,” are proud fruits of purposeful women’s work. The hustle and bustle in these public houses is among the most original and honorable things Zurich can offer.

Crowds flock to and from these, in which even Zurich’s class differences seem to want to blur. Families who used to concentrate their summer excursions on a pompous two-horse Küchlifahrt to the Nidelbad or the nearby Waid no longer stand out where the free, cheerful sense for nature in school and home, among boys and girls, is energetically awakened, despite complaints about restricting scientific education.

Water Supply. The first pipe well was built in 1430 at Rennweg. Around the middle of the 19th century, seven wellworks supplied the city with 110 (plus 7 in the city district itself) mostly wooden-capped springs hourly 36,000 Maß (about 1.5 liters each); the associated pipe network was 90,000 feet long. In addition, there were many soda wells, some of very doubtful quality. There were also pumping stations in the Limmat, in the Schipfe, and at the Schanzengraben (G. Meyer von Knonau, Der Kanton Zürich, 1844). From 1860 onwards, systematic investigations for a rational water supply were carried out and, based on a 1867 report by Bürkli, recognized as a classic, it was fundamentally decided that the existing springs were to be refitted and a new 30-hp pumping station from the Limmat for service water at the upper Mühlesteg was to be built by the city.
Zurich: The Grossmünster.
Construction began in 1868: two reservoirs at the Polytechnic and Schmelzberg above the observatory; filter in the Limmat bed below the Bauschanze and from there a cement pipe to the pumping station.

A daily consumption of 135-190 liters per inhabitant was calculated. Already in 1872, there was too little service water. A new pumping station was provisionally built at Platzspitz, which (completed 1870) together with the old one could pump 15,000 m³ daily. But even this was soon too little. In 1875 the construction of a definitive water plant at the Letten was decided. The Limmat was dammed at Drahtschmidli by a needle weir and through a canal a water power of 900 hp was generated, which allowed a maximum water lift of 51,000 m³ per day.

The plant was completed in 1879, initially with power also delivered directly by wire ropes. For the service water, previously held in a special section of the reservoir at the Polytechnic, a separate reservoir was built at Langensteinen (Oberstrass)—the dam closure still stands today—and above the little castle on the Zurichberg, a third drinking water reservoir for the high-pressure zone was built at 145 m above the lake level.

Then in 1884 a severe typhus epidemic broke out in Zurich. It was generally suspected that the cause of its rapid spread lay in an infection of the water supply. Indeed, the cement pipe in the Limmat was badly damaged and almost clogged in one place. This led to the establishment of an “extended water commission,” whose members included Dr. K. Zehnder and Dr. H. v. Wyss as doctors, Prof. Cramer as bacteriologist, Prof. Lunge as chemist, and Prof. Heim as geologist.

Thorough studies of the whole water supply issue led to the result that lake water should be maintained as the main drinking water (besides numerous already existing spring intakes), but the point of water intake should be moved 200 meters farther above the quays, where the water is drawn at a depth of 12 m and led by an iron pipe through Schanzengraben-Sihl to a filter plant at Sihlquai and from there to the Letten pumping station.

Chemically and bacterially, the lake water proved favorable: alkalinity in French hardness degrees 12.5; organic substance 18.2–23.5 mg per liter, free ammonia and nitric acid traces, albuminoid ammonia 0.035–0.05 mg per liter, fungal germs 200 per cm³ in raw, 20 in filtered water.

Construction work began in 1885, the new filter plant was put into operation in 1886, and the satisfaction was experienced that since the introduction of the new great filtration plant (sand and gravel filter in 10 chambers) the typhus case rate per 10,000 inhabitants fell from an average of 62.88 to 8.27, and mortality from 6.67 to 0.8, aligning with the minimum rates for larger cities with favorable sanitary conditions.
Zurich: The Kreuzkirche, Neumünster.

Although this new large drinking water supply now functioned perfectly in quality, it soon quantitatively no longer met the demand due to rapid population growth. In 1905 the average water consumption per capita per day was given as 220 liters, with a maximum of 315 liters. To increase the number of public fountains in the city and to build fountains in newly emerging quarters, from 1907 onward much of the richly productive Sihl and Lorze springs began to be supplied.
Zurich: The Church of Enge.

They arise on blue, sticky-tough basic moraine clay of the 1st ice age in a similar manner from the 30-40 m high covering gravel conglomerate of the Sihl and Lorze valleys at Sihlsprung-Menzingen, as in small scale the hotel spring on the Uto peak (see geology in the article Zurich, canton). A large, rainy (1,600 mm), mostly wooded catchment area and the magnificent natural filter apparatus of the porous Nagelfluh plate create a very constant yield, whose maxima and minima fluctuate only in a ratio of 5:3.

The Sihl springs are connected by an 11.5 km long pipe line with up to 40 cm diameter; the Lorze springs by a 5.7 km long, up to 50 cm wide pipe line to Sihlbrugg; from there, a 17.7 km long, 55 cm wide pipe with 2.5‰ gradient runs through the Sihl valley to the new reservoir near Albisgütli (500 m above sea level = 91 m above lake level). Here, the water (in the normal rainfall year 1905, about 20,400 liters per minute) is distributed to the supply lines for the public spring water fountains and to the medium and low-pressure pipeline zones of the lake water system.

The facility cost a total of 3,174,104 francs and supplies over half of the entire water requirement of the city. In quality, the water of the Sihl-Lorze springs is very good: in 1905 it showed temperatures of 8.6 (January) to 10.9°C (September) and a bacterial count of 0–37. Nevertheless, it is somewhat hard with 24–25 French degrees compared to lake water (13), so soda addition is necessary for steam boiler feed. The Sihl valley springs have supplied the city since December 4, and those from the Lorze valley since November 25, 1902. Still, with continued population growth in Zurich, a larger water intake facility—either from the lake or from suitable groundwater areas—must be considered in the next few years.

The total city water consumption from October 1, 1906, to September 30, 1907, amounted to 14,700,098 m³. Of this, 67.6% fell on the low-pressure zone, 27.3% on the medium-pressure zone, 4.1% on the high-pressure zone, and 1% on the upper high-pressure zone. This results in an average consumption of 237 (maximum 330) liters per head per day. A revenue of CHF 1,751,000 was generated from the supplied water (including for public use), which means over half a million in net profit after 3% depreciation. The entire pipeline network for service, operating, and drinking water was 128 km long at the end of 1907 (excluding spring water pipelines). In addition, there was the 2.67 km long 900 mm diameter intake pipe from the lake to the filters and 0.51 km from the filter to the pumping station.

Ahead of these generous drinking water supply facilities, a sewer system had to be provided, for which engineer Bürkli had already designed the plan and whose expansion with the bucket system (replacing the old open ditches) started in 1867. Today it runs through the entire city and (including some suction areas) flows below the city (by government decree below the water supply plant at Letten) into the Limmat.
About hospitals (cantonal, municipal and private voluntary) and the excellent social care for poor patients by various aid institutions, see further below.

Epidemics. Cholera last affected Zurich in 1867. Among the general funds of Zurich city foundations still exists a “Fund for Assistance in Cholera Epidemics.” Typhus is no longer endemic; the last epidemic in 1884 led to thorough sanitation of the drinking water supply. However, scarlet fever and diphtheria are constantly present, although the latter disease appears less dangerous due to modern serum treatment than in earlier times. For restricting these schoolhouse hazards, many parents apparently lack insight and authorities effective legislation to enforce, despite existing free bacterial examinations and compulsory free disinfection of furniture, clothing, and rooms in cases of scarlet fever, diphtheria, as well as typhus, smallpox, and puerperal fever (optionally for tuberculosis). In 1907, 462 scarlet fever cases and 417 diphtheria cases led to 1,265 school exclusions.
The scarlet fever frequency in previous years was as follows: 1906 = 505; 1905 = 1,050; 1904 = 961; 1903 = 1,174;

Diphtheria 1906 = 467; 1905 = 427; 1904 = 344; 1903 = 238. Other infectious diseases reported in 1907: no smallpox; tetanus 16 cases; measles 215 (1906 = 1,217; 1905 = 60; 1904 = 1,234; 1903 = 21); typhus 46 (1906 = 47; 1905 = 59; 1904 = 83; 1903 = 41); puerperal fever 23; other infectious diseases 120; total 1,511 cases.

Eye and ear examinations of schoolchildren were reported in the section on education (Canton Zurich). A free school dental clinic has recently been established. Mortality is also treated in the section on health care. Burial is also worth mentioning. It is carried out at the city's expense. In 1907, 1,614 burials were carried out at a daily maximum of 16. Zurich has a total of 18 cemeteries, namely: District I: Cemetery Sihlfeld (central cemetery, with crematorium and outstanding monuments) and cemetery on the High Promenade (no longer in operation; partly body preservation due to clayey moraine soil);

Our chapter on the hygienic conditions of the city of Zurich may suitably conclude with the quote: “Zurich is thus one of the healthiest cities in Switzerland.”

7. Transport routes.

The traffic lines converging at Zurich main station have already been mentioned at the beginning. It remains to add here that besides the main station in the Zurich city area, the following railway stations also facilitate traffic: Wiedikon, Enge, and Wollishofen on the left bank lake railway, Letten, Stadelhofen, and Tiefenbrunnen on the right bank. At the Selnau station, Uetliberg and Sihl valley railways converge; the former (opened 1875) climbs steeply by adhesion railway via the stations Binz and Waldegg in a wide curve towards the west after a half-hour ride to the Uetliberg summit, the latter leads through Giesshübel-Brunau-Manegg-Sod-Adliswil into the Sihl valley and connects at Sihlbrugg with the federal railway line Thalwil-Zug.

Before railway connections (opening of the first line from Zurich to Baden on August 9, 1847, the second to Winterthur on May 16, 1855, to Uster on August 1, 1856, to Zug on June 1, 1864, etc.) existed, steamship routes operated on Lake Zurich. Already on May 19, 1835, the first steamship ran. In 1891, local traffic on the lake was significantly promoted by the introduction of “Dampfschwalben,” which give the lower part of the lake a splendidly pulsating life today, while the courses of the large steamers were relatively reduced due to double railway service.
There are still two postal routes: one to Maur and one to Zumikon. Zurich has 19 post and 17 telegraph offices.
Zurich: Swiss National Museum.

Within the city itself, a far-reaching and rapidly expanding network of streetcars facilitates traffic. The first line was opened as a private horse tramway on September 24, 1882. Hardly a decade later, the first electrically operated line arose to Burgwies, and in 1898, the power plant connected with the pumping station in Letten became operational so that the entire tramway network could be placed in municipal electric operation. Soon the central Zurichberg railway and the streetcar of the industrial district were also annexed by purchase. Today, private tramways still exist: the line from Giesshübel to Albisgütli, the Limmat Valley streetcar from Marienstrasse to Altstetten-Schlieren-Dietikon (from here tram over Mutschellen to Bremgarten)-Unterengstringen-Kloster Fahr-Weiningen, as well as lines from the main station or Wipkingen to Hoengg and from Leonhardsplatz to Oerlikon-Seebach-Glattbrugg with a branch to Schwamendingen. In addition, three cable railways to the heights of the Zurichberg: from Rigiplatz to Rigiviertel, from Leonhardsplatz to the Polytechnic, and from Römerhof to Waldhaus Dolder, with subsequent streetcar to the Grand Hotel Dolder.
Zurich: The Urania public observatory.

The total length of the municipal streetcar network was 29.8 km at the end of 1907, with 59.4 km of track length altogether (partially double track), with 133 motor and 32 trailer cars. The entire network is divided into six operation lines, whose cars are identified by colored number plates. Daily frequency in 1907: 62,136 persons. Other means of transport include some taxi-meter motor carriages and the ordinary cab service; the latter has been significantly improved by prizes awarded by the traffic association. Numerous motor, rowing, and sailing boats can be rented on the lake, and large barges pass on goods traffic (notably building material transport from sandstone quarries and gravel pits of the upper Lake Zurich).

Zurich counted 941 streets and squares in 1907. Due to rapid city expansion on the periphery, numerous new ones are added annually. Entire street sections arise on the slopes of the Zurichberg, where the old wild brook valleys are artificially filled or dammed over. Thus, the Wolfbach, which flowed from Hottingen into the Limmat at the upper Mühlesteg, has disappeared entirely from sight, as has the Klosbach and the Hornbach is dammed; the niche of the former Lindenbach in District 4 almost disappeared.

At night, the city is brightly illuminated by gas lights and on larger squares and main traffic arteries by electric arc lamps. Gas lighting was introduced by a private company in 1856. In 1886, the city took over this task. Today's gas pipeline network reaches to the outermost boundaries of the city, even up to the Uetliberg ridge. Everything is fed from the municipal gasworks in Schlieren, a model plant first-rate in its construction and operation. In December 1908, it delivered 105,000 to 106,000 m³ of gas daily with a daily coal consumption of 35 wagons.

Thanks to its recently completed expansion with a parallel plant (already foreseen in the first construction opened in 1898) with vertical retorts and wagon dumper, it has become significantly more powerful. Annual output in 1907 = 26,640,200 m³, of which private consumption and gas delivery to adjacent municipalities (Adliswil, Oerlikon, Zollikon, Kilchberg, Schlieren, Albisrieden-Altstetten) accounted for 22,162,889 m³. These numbers are rapidly increasing; increase from 1906 to 1907 = over 12%. Gas consumption per capita per year for City of Zurich and above municipalities: 114.02 m³.
