8. Intellectual Life — Associations.

Intellectual life culminates publicly in the political conditions of our pronounced democracy. If one wanted to dissect a bit, the Zurichers would have to be divided into two categories: active (engaged in politics) and passive (in part pushed in, in part indifferent), and the first category would split again into two rubrics: serious workers on the community, full of courage and willingness for sacrifice, and just as industrious political strivers.

A glance at the city Zurich’s daily on a Saturday before a vote or election day would not find this division entirely inaccurate: The first pages of the daily, swollen to 40 or more folio pages, contain the briefly held official announcements (the daily is also the city gazette). Then follows full- and half-page calls from political party committees, often pleading with the same, especially those taken from compliant statistics, motives for black, white, and red.

After that come column- and page-wide valuable advertisements pro and contra, mostly supported by a flood of colored leaflets, distributed on the busiest streets and placed in all mailboxes. For important events, some parties even deploy velvet with zeal and music to the ballot. This must seem strange to a foreigner accustomed to a monarchical state system, yet certain solemnity, expressed in the self-determination of the individual, cannot be missed, and the order with which everything usually transpires inspires respect.

Newspapers and periodicals currently (1909) appear in Zurich numbering about 160, of which 9 daily, 1 weekly thrice, 3 weekly twice, 53 weekly once, 41 fortnightly, and 33 monthly once. Already in 1666 a weekly paper appeared; the Friday weekly, today Zürcher Freitagszeitung (Bürklizitig, circulation 3,500), dates back to 1673 and is probably the oldest Swiss newspaper. The Zürcher Zeitung was first published on January 12, 1780; since 1821 it has been called Neue Zürcher Zeitung; it appeared daily since 1843, for several years thrice daily, with a circulation of 15,000. As early as 1801, the paper must have been very loyal to the government because its publisher then asked the government governor to partially exempt it from censorship, as he had entrusted the Helvetic articles to a man "of whom there is absolutely no concern that he would take up anything contrary to the spirit or sense of the government" (Max Uebelhör: Zur Geschichte der Neuen Zürcher Zeitung 1803–1821, in N.Z.Z. of March 31, 1908).

The city Zurich daily (official gazette, circulation 27,000) has existed since 1837. Among the most widely circulated daily papers are also: Zürcher Post, Tagesanzeiger (circulation 62,000), Grütlianer, Volksrecht, and Neue Zürcher Nachrichten (as organ of the Catholics). Original ephemeral features in the newspaper literature are the Sechseläuten sheets, in which local events of the year are usually presented in word and image with more or less wit and humor. As a permanent weekly political satirical paper appearing in Zurich since 1874, the Nebelspalter deserves mention. More details can be found in the commemorative publication for the Zurich press jubilee 1908 (Contributions to the history of the Zurich press).
Zurich: The City Theatre.

The “Associations and Societies” rubric in the new Zurich city address book gives an approximate idea of the great space that association life occupies in our city and of the manifold opportunities offered to our population on the soil of public charitable work, for further education in countless fields, as well as for the cultivation of joyful sociability, mutual support, and the exercise of all kinds of sports.

Among the approximately one thousand registered associations and societies (and some influential groups may have escaped registration—editor's note.), we find 163 professional associations, 2 burial societies, 16 dramatic associations, 161 charitable associations and institutions, 92 singing societies, 69 social clubs, 101 sick and support societies and death benefit funds, 40 art and scientific societies, 20 military societies, 37 music societies, 36 political societies, 14 district associations, 42 religious societies, 1 chess club, 67 shooting clubs, 54 sports clubs, 3 shorthand clubs, 30 student fraternities and academic specialty clubs, 32 gymnastic clubs, and 21 guild societies. Moreover, most larger associations have numerous branch sections not included in the above numbers, which also have active activity in some special area. (N.Z.Z. 11/II 09).

Considerable libraries are maintained by some of these societies and associations, as well as by state and community. A central library is eagerly sought; in the meanwhile, a central card catalog exists in the Helmhaus, and the individual libraries combine the announcement of their new acquisitions in a common, periodically published growth directory. The following institutions participate: Cantonal and university library (in the choir of the Predigerkirche, 95,000 volumes, 150,000 dissertations and brochures, 1,000 manuscripts), city library (in the Wasserkirche at Helmhaus, over 175,000 catalog titles, 4,300 volumes of manuscripts and numerous incunabula, 80,000 view sheets, 11,000 maps, 17,000 coins), library of the Museum of Applied Arts (at National Museum), the Swiss National Museum, the federal polytechnic school (45,000 titles), cantonal military library (police barracks), state archives, libraries of the law, medical-surgical (both in the choir of the Predigerkirche), and natural science society (last at Helmhaus, about 25,000 volumes, society founded by Johann Gessner 1747), Pestalozzianum, art society, museum society (latter in the "Museum" opposite the meat hall, large reading room with 120 newspapers and 650 magazines, founded 1834). Many scientific, artistic, and social societies also have their own libraries (academic reading association of both universities, reading circle Hottingen, Alpine Club, numerous singing societies, reading circles, etc.). Recently, a library of the central office for social literature of Switzerland with reading room at Seilergraben also exists.
Zurich: Tonhalle.

Of great benefit also are the public libraries and reading rooms of the Pestalozzi society for popular education and popular instruction, which reported 210,000 visitors in 1907 in 10 branches across the whole city. The society also organizes several popular lectures and concerts annually in winter; expenses in 1907 nearly 45,000 francs, of which the city contributed 21,000 francs. In general, the number of public lectures is extraordinarily large in winter, almost too numerous.

Outstanding collections: Swiss National Museum (already mentioned). Museum of Applied Arts of the city of Zurich (changing modern exhibitions, spatial art). Collections in the federal Polytechnic: archaeological collection, zoological (including original developmental history specimens [snails by A. Lang]), mineralogical (D. Wiser's collection), petrographic (originals by Grubenmann), geological (first original collection for general geology, especially phenomena of mountain pressure, by Heim) and paleontological collections (Heer and Mayer-Eymar originals, Santiago Roth's collection of Pampas mammals, mammoth from Niederweningen); collection in the agricultural and forestry school (zoological with interesting originals on the history of domestic animals by C. Keller, botanical according to general principles by C. Schröter). Splendid reliefs of Switzerland by Becker, Simon, Imfeld, Heim.
Zurich: Albisgütli.

Copper engraving cabinet. Collection of the geographic-ethnographic society (Seilergraben). Pestalozzianum (permanent school exhibition, temporarily in the Wollenhof at Schipfe). Municipal zoological museum, formerly Nageli Museum, at Zurichhorn (Swiss mammals and birds). Finally, mention should be made of the botanical garden with its collections and the public aviary with live birds at Mythenquai. A zoological garden is missing.

A worthy building (art house) is now being built for fine arts at Heimplatz, while its old home, the Künstlergütli opposite the south front of the Polytechnic, has to make way for the new university building. The permanent exhibition of the Zurich Art Society houses valuable pieces, especially by the two famous Zurich painters Rudolf Koller and Arnold Böcklin. Changing exhibitions of modern masters are held meanwhile in the “Künstlerhaus,” a provisional barrack near the stock exchange. Many valuable paintings are in private Zurich possession and could not be generally accessible in the previously tight premises, but are to be exhibited in the new art house.

Much more domestic than fine arts has been theater and concerts in Zurich. For years, acting in the City Theatre and on its drama stage Pfauen Theater under Alfred Reucker's direction has deserved full praise. Kapellmeister Lothar Kempter has earned great merits in opera. It was a rightly recognized and worthily carried out task to help bring Wagner’s operas in progressing order at the very place of Wagner's earlier activity to continuous enthusiastic reception. In the Tonhalle, Friedrich Hegar has over a lifetime masterfully brought the most exalted creations of old and new masters (Beethoven, Brahms, Richard Strauss) to performances with orchestra and choirs.

The high musical understanding commonly credited to the Zurich public is essentially a feat of artistic education by Zurich masters, whose line, starting with Baumgartner, runs over Ignaz Heim, Gustav Weber, Friedrich Hegar, Karl Attenhofer, Gottfried Angerer to the very modern Volkmar Andreae, all excelling as orchestra and choir conductors as well as composers. In recent years, performances at the City Theatre and Tonhalle have also become accessible to the less affluent in special, excellently organized people’s performances and popular concerts. Moreover, several other theaters cater to fans of lighter muses: the Central Theater on Weinbergstrasse (farces, cinematograph, etc.), the Corso Theater at the old Tonhalle square (variety), the intimate theater in the Urania (cabaret).

Often scientific, theatrical, musical, or similar events serve charitable purposes—recall for example in 1908/09 the concerts of the singers' association “Harmonie” for the fire victims of Bonaduz, the “Men’s Choir Zurich” for farmers affected by the snow damage in May, and for the earthquake victims in Messina, for which the Natural Science Society held a town hall lecture. Thus, in intellectual life, noble striving for education and selfless sharing in implementing charitable tasks often effectively interlace.

But the Zurich Tonhalle is not only the center of musical life, around which countless musical societies are devoted with their regular internal performances. It is also the center of social life, in summer on the scenic terrace during excellent nightly garden concerts where Kapellmeister Kempter even dares to perform symphonies, and in winter for all kinds of events, from charity bazaars to the elegant costume parties of the Hottingen reading circle and the polytechnic academy, as well as from the dance evenings of the largest clubs to the annual large masked ball. Up to 3,000 persons have assembled in cheerful merriment in the hospitable rooms. But sad tones and serious words have also sounded in these art-dedicated rooms when it was necessary to honor great deceased or boldly gather in the name of the fatherland.
[Dr. Leo Wehrli.]
9. Church System.

The unification of Zurich with its suburbs in 1893 left the church parishes unaffected. Therefore, there are still the following 13 Protestant parishes today: Grossmünster, Fraumünster, St. Peter, Predigern, Aussersihl, Enge, Fluntern, Neumünster, Oberstrass, Unterstrass, Wiedikon, Wipkingen, Wollishofen. In addition, there is the French parish affiliated with the evangelical state church and the state-recognized Old Catholic parish. Among private religious communities are the Evangelical-Lutheran Kreuzgemeinde, the Roman Catholic parishes St. Peter and Paul and Unterstrass-Zurich, the episcopal Methodist church, the Israelite religious community, etc.
10. Organization of Administration.

The administrative organization of the city of Zurich has differed from that of other Zurich municipalities since 1893, in which the unification of the old town with the suburbs gave legal sanction to the development into a metropolis, not inconsiderably. The communal assembly in the form of a traditional landsgemeinde ceased to exist in Zurich from this time; however, the totality of voting Swiss citizens domiciled in the city (the “community”) still exercises considerable influence on the conduct of municipal administration via the ballot. Such rights initially include the most important elections: city president, small city council, large city council, central school board, district school boards, primary and secondary schoolteachers, debt collection officers, and justices of the peace. Furthermore, the “community” must vote by mandatory referendum on the community ordinance, on resolutions of the large city council involving recurrent annual expenditure of more than 20,000 Fr. or one-time expenditures of more than 200,000 Fr. The optional referendum applies to all other resolutions of the large city council except elections, acceptance of accounts and management report, budget, setting of tax rates, and resolutions adopted with urgency clause. A referendum is deemed valid if requested within 20 days by 2,000 voters. Besides the referendum, there is the right of initiative: any qualified voter can submit a motion to the large city council, which must be submitted to a public vote if it falls within the community’s competence and if supported by 30 members of the large city council or 2,000 voters.
Zurich: Escher Monument at Bahnhofplatz.

The large city council is elected in the five city districts for a term of three years. It currently consists of 125 members. Its most important functions are: election of cantonal jurors, tax commission, orphanage board, and several other committees; setting of the budget and tax rates; supervision of the entire city administration; approval of the annual accounts; enactment of ordinances; review of submissions to the community, etc.
The city council consists of nine members, each heading an administrative department. The nine departments are:
1) Administrative department of the city president;
2) Finance;
3) Taxation;
4) Police;
5) Health;
6) Construction I (civil and structural engineering);
7) Construction II (industrial enterprises);
8) School system;
9) Guardianship system.

As a collegium, the city council prepares all submissions to be sent to the large city council and the community, executes their resolutions, carries out elections not assigned to other authorities, etc. For school administration, besides the city council, but under the chairmanship of one of its members, there is the central school board (25 members), which submits proposals on some important matters (such as the organization of the school system) directly to the large city council, but otherwise only prepares matters for the small city council. Supervision of the public school in the individual city districts is performed by the district school boards.

12. Health Care.

For public health care, the municipality has a number of partly preventive, partly repressive institutions. Among the first primarily counts food control, managed by 9 veterinarians, a permanent sanitary corps, and a municipal laboratory, covering all foodstuffs and the most important luxury items. The city also operates a number of lake and river bathing establishments. To improve housing in hygienic and economic respects, the municipality approved 2.5 million Fr. in April 1907 for the construction of housing by the city. Human excrements are discharged by the municipal bucket system; household refuse is burned in the municipal refuse incineration plant. However, effective combat of the health hazards of prostitution is lacking. Among repressive measures are compulsory disinfection in cases of scarlet fever, diphtheria, typhus, smallpox, epidemic tetanus, and puerperal fever.

For outpatient treatment of poor residents, around 24,000 Fr. were spent in 1907, and 164 persons were cared for in the municipal emergency hospital. The construction of a special city hospital is planned. Private health care operates a number of hospitals. Notable are the Zurich Children's Hospital, the Red Cross Sisters’ House, the Nursing Asylum and Diaconesses’ Institute Neumünster, the Theodosianum, the Swiss institute for epileptics, the Swiss nurses' school with women's hospital, all based on charitable foundations. In addition, there are several private clinics run by doctors. See the article on the canton Zurich for the cantonal hospital. 13. Charitable Work.

Of the large number of charitable institutions, only the following should be highlighted: Various associations existing in the individual quarters, such as the charitable societies of Enge, Wiedikon, Neumünster, Unterstrass, Wipkingen, and the Zurich aid society, pursue general goals of charity. These corporations usually also are the protectors of institutions of all kinds. For example, the Zurich aid society operates or protects a savings bank, a general health insurance, a blind and deaf-mute institution, a nursery, while the charitable society Neumünster can show such areas of activity as a savings bank, an old-age asylum, nursery schools, an apprentice home, the protection of single women, etc.

Special care for women and children is the aim of the Zurich section of the Swiss charitable Women's Association; it operates a girls' nursery, several crèches, a household school, supports the authorities in supervising the care of foster children, etc. Purposes of youth care are also pursued by the Zurich Child Protection Association, which offers help to morally endangered, neglected, abused children, as well as the city's holiday colonies and milk cures, which send a large number of children in need of convalescence to the countryside every year or seek to strengthen them by administering milk. Finally, the apprenticeship sponsorship Zurich enables poor boys and girls to learn a craft.

Practical reforms in the field of alcohol issues have been realized by the Women’s Association for Temperance and Public Welfare by setting up and operating a number of alcohol-free eateries in various parts of the city. Special night shelters are especially the two institutions of the Salvation Army designed for the very poorest. Popular education is devoted to by the Pestalozzi society through operation of 8 public reading rooms and a public library with branches, through popular scientific lectures and courses, publishing of writings, folk concerts.
14. Social-Political Institutions.

For the peaceful settlement of collective labor disputes, a conciliation office consisting of three members exists; for job placement, a municipal employment office. In winter, an unemployment commission operates, which, for example, supported 298 unemployed persons with a total of 28,388 Fr. in 1906/1907. For housing registration, there is a special office that publishes a bulletin twice weekly. By municipal resolution of April 21, 1907, construction of housing by the city was also started, with a credit of 2.4 million Fr. approved for this purpose.

The city also strives to set a good example in its treatment of workers. It introduced the nine-hour day as the maximum working time, as well as a minimum wage of 5 Fr. 50 Rp. for skilled and 5 Fr. for unskilled workers. Every employee and worker is also entitled to an annual recreation leave of at least four days. Also worth mentioning are school meals, on which about 47,000 Fr. was spent in 1907. Additionally, clothing costs for poor pupils were 5,407 Fr. There are about 50 municipal kindergartens and 26 youth nurseries. The former are attended by over 1,800, the latter by about 800 children. Baths exist in 25 schools. School health care is led by a permanent school doctor. A special school dental clinic exists.
[Dr. E. Grossmann.]
15. Prehistory.

The area of the city of Zurich was continuously inhabited since the Neolithic period. Besides numerous individual finds from the younger Stone Age, four pile dwellings were discovered in the city area: in the large and small Hafner, in the Bauschanze, and in the Haumesser. All these settlements persisted until the end of the Bronze Age, in which period especially the Haumesser pile dwelling near Wollishofen developed. Even then, people already lived on solid land, and a refuge arose on the Uetliberg. In the Iron Age, the pile dwellings near Zurich were abandoned; however, the fortified Lindenhof was densely populated, and the Uetliberg refuge was richly equipped with ramparts and ditches.

The dead were first buried in burial mounds, as could be investigated in Burghölzli. Later, uncremated bodies were buried in free earth. Such graves, assigned to the 2nd Iron Age (La Tène period), were found in Enge's Entibühl, on Rebhügel, and near the new church Wiedikon, at Bäckerstrasse in Zurich III, and on the Uetliberg. An important find recently unearthed during railway construction at the border to Altstetten was a golden bowl of chased work and a technique making the piece unique. It probably comes from a princely grave of the 7th century BC.

Zurich must also have been a mint, as a large treasure of fused coins made of potin, found near today’s stock exchange, proves. Zurich was certainly one of the 400 villages or one of the 12 cities the Helvetians burned during their emigration.

In Roman times, Zurich was a customs station. This was located under the protection of the castrum, which was found on the Lindenhof and was in optical connection with the watchtower on the Uetliberg. On or near the Lindenhof, the brickworks stand, which marked its ware with D.S.P. and was interpreted by Mommsen as Doliare Stationis Publicae (Bricks of the public customs office). On the Lindenhof a Roman inscription stone was found in 1747 bearing the old name of Zurich (Turicum). It is a gravestone set by the customs chief for his son.

Another inscription stone found in Zurich speaks of a guild of bear hunters. Roman Turicum was located around the Lindenhof. A building with mosaic floor stood near today's Peterskirche, another near the Wasserkirche. In Oetenbach a Roman gold jewel was discovered, and coin treasures were found in Rennweg and other places. Similar finds were made in the former outer municipalities of Zurich. In Enge’s Sternen, remains of a Roman settlement were found. Another Roman settlement was found at the gallows near Albisrieden; a third below the Waid near Wipkingen. Roman graves were found, besides the mentioned tombstone of L. Ael. Urbicus, on the Lindenhof, at Zentralhof, Münsterhof, Tiefenhöfe, and Sihlfeld.

The Roman road from Baden (Aquae) stretched through Zurich via Rennweg into the castrum, then went down Strehlgasse, crossed the Limmat at what is now the meat hall, and runs further upstream today under the name “alte Landstrasse” towards Zollikon. Along it, Roman coins were repeatedly found.
Zurich: Sechseläuten. The burning of the “Böög.”

In early Germanic times, the Lindenhof was the seat of the imperial palace, and around it, the city extended, near which a number of farms cited in documents in the 8th and 9th centuries lay, which gradually grew into separate municipalities or were merged with the city, such as Wipkingen, Wiedikon, Stadelhofen, Riesbach, Hirslanden, Hottingen, Fluntern.

Apart from the ancient population center on the Lindenhof, new centers had formed in early Christian times around the Gross- and Fraumünster, until about the 10th century all three were enclosed by a wall into a “city.” The graves from Alemannic-Frankish times are interesting. Already in the barrows at Burghölzli, Alemanni were buried. An Alemannic cemetery was almost simultaneously discovered at Entibühl above Balgrist, yielding finds from Alemannic times, including jewelry and weapons. In the last decade, two new Alemannic cemeteries could be investigated: the one at Rebhügel Wiedikon and the large cemetery at Bäckerstrasse in Zurich III. The finds from these graves are in the Swiss National Museum and are of great interest. A Frankish grave was characterized by the deceased being given the favorite weapon of the Franks, the throwing axe or francisca. Several times, mother and child lay together. In one such grave, remains of a wooden coffin were found, within which a richly decorated woman with a small child in her left arm lay. Apparently, mother and child were buried simultaneously.

The woman wore a necklace of glass, amber, and enamel beads. Two gold brooches with inlaid almandines lay on her chest. On the right side of the head was an animal bone: food had been given to the deceased. In the belt area were found a silver-plated buckle, two silver and gilded snake-head brooches with niello inlays. The child’s arm also appears to have worn bead jewelry. Toys were also given to the child in the grave. Next to the woman’s left thigh lay the remains of a little box containing toiletries.
[Dr. J. Heierli.]

Zurichberg

(Canton and district Zurich). 679 m. A broad hill ridge, consisting of horizontal layers of freshwater molasse, extending approximately 5 km lengthwise from SE to NW and spreading between Lake Zurich and the Glatt valley. The upper part is forested, through which the Beautification Association has laid paths crisscrossing so that it now contains very popular walks. The molasse layers are here and there covered by thin coatings of erratic boulders. The northern end of the Zurichberg is marked by the broad saddle through which the road from Zurich to Oerlikon passes (481 m), and the southern end by the Zurich-Witikon road (617 m).
Lake Zurich as seen from Uetliberg.
Zurichhorn

(Canton, district, and municipality Zurich). 410 m. Delta at the mouth of the Hornbach into Lake Zurich, where the city's quays at the right lake shore end. A magnificent park with a restaurant has been laid out there.
Lake Zurich

(Cantons Zurich, Schwyz, and St. Gallen). Lake Zurich is the fourth largest of all Swiss lakes. It is embedded entirely like Lake Constance in molasse and thus lacks the charm of the high mountains like that even though not to the same degree since the “Upper Lake” has already approached the considerable pre-Alpine peaks Hirzli, Schänniserberg, and Speer quite closely. Because of its gentle shores and many idyllic bays, it has been called the loveliest of the Swiss lakes.
Lake Zurich: ephemeral island east of the Stäfner stone at lowest water level (March 12, 1909).

1. Name. The earliest mention of Lake Zurich can be found in the Vita St. Galli of the 8th century, where it is called lacus de Turegum. Later (1250), it is called lacus Turicinus; but as early as 1286, the name Zürichse appears for the first time, which has remained as “Zürichsee” (Lake Zurich) to the present. The designation “Zürichersee” on newer maps is evidently only a creation by analogy, similar to Zugersee, Genfersee, etc., but is nowhere spoken or otherwise written.

2. Maps. The oldest depiction of Lake Zurich is found on the Swiss map of Tschudi (1538), albeit with many inaccuracies. Already better is the delineation on the map of the Zurich region by Joost Murer (1566). Much more precise is our lake on the excellent Gyger map (1667) at the scale of 1:32,000. An even model representation is the Dufour map (1834–1864) at the scale 1:100,000. The surveys for it were done in the lake area from 1843–1851 by engineer J. Wild and later published in 1:25,000 in the Siegfried Atlas. The depth soundings (first exact sounding of a major Swiss lake) were conducted for 1,210 points in the main Lake Zurich and 460 points in the upper lake, i.e., 19.2 points per km². (Lake Geneva 20.8; Lake Constance 20.7; Neuchâtel Lake 9.7 points per km²). The most precise lake shore map was compiled by the Zurich government in 1850–52 at 1:1,000. This unpublished so-called lake map (in 59 sheets) is still used today to record all changes in lake shores. A handy relief-tone map was published in recent years by Kümmerly and Frey in Bern at 1:50,000.

Political municipality of the canton of Zurich, cantonal capital and district capital, located at the outflow of the Limmat from Lake Zurich between the Albis ridge in the west and Adlisberg and Zurichberg in the east. Around 200 statio Turicensis/Turicum, 680-700 Ziurichi, French Zurich, Italian Zurigo, Romansh Turitg.

After late Celtic and Roman beginnings, the city, located at the intersection of navigable routes and land paths, developed from the early medieval, partly fortified settlement cores of Lindenhof hill and Fraumünster-Münsterhof on the left as well as Niederdorf and Grossmünster on the right bank of the Limmat. These were enclosed in the 12th century by an extensive city wall, newly built in the 13th century; Stadelhof remained outside the wall. The construction of the baroque star-shaped fortifications in the 17th century led to an expansion of the fortified settlement area. With the municipal merger of 1893, the municipalities of Aussersihl, Enge, Fluntern, Hirslanden, Hottingen, Leimbach, Oberstrass, Riesbach, Unterstrass, Wiedikon, Wipkingen, and Wollishofen became part of the city. In 1934, Affoltern bei Zürich, Albisrieden, Altstetten, Höngg, Oerlikon, Schwamendingen, Seebach, and Witikon followed.

Zurich is home to federal institutions (ETH and National Museum), private (Tamedia) and public media companies (Swiss Radio and Television), as well as international football (FIFA) and ice hockey (IIHF) organizations. As the economic center of Switzerland, the city hosts numerous banks and financial service providers such as UBS, Credit Suisse Group (Schweizerische Kreditanstalt), Swiss Re (Swiss Reinsurance Company), Swiss Life (Pension Institution), and Zurich Financial Services (Zurich Insurance), national firms like Migros, as well as internationally active companies such as IBM Switzerland, Google, Siemens (Siemens-Albis), and Asea Brown Boveri (ABB).

From Prehistory to the High Middle Ages
Prehistory

The oldest settlement indications on city territory are flint tools from the Mesolithic found at Katzensee. Numerous finds on and in the lower lake basin testify to significant settlement during the Neolithic and Bronze Age in the period from about 4300 to 800 BC. The oldest pile dwelling finds originate from the former island Kleiner Hafner in front of Bellevue. Remains of prehistoric land settlements are only sporadically recorded. At Letten and near Rathausbrücke, metal objects from the Bronze Age were found in the Limmat, possibly deposited there as votive offerings. In the Hallstatt and early La Tène periods, a significant central settlement was located on the Uetliberg. Burial mounds from this period examined in Höngg, Balgrist and Burghölzli contained burials with partly rich grave goods. From the early and middle La Tène period, sporadic grave finds are known within the city area.
Late La Tène period, Roman era, Merovingian period

On the left side of the Limmat, on the moraine hill with the elevations Lindenhof, St. Petershügel and the today dismantled Sihlbühl in the north, a Celtic oppidum is verifiable from 80 BC onwards, in which a wealthy leadership class among other things operated a mint. The puzzling find of a lump consisting of over 17,000 fused Celtic coins from around 100 BC, which was uncovered on the southern Bahnhofstrasse, suggests a votive deposit in water.
Pair of bird-shaped fibulae from the richly furnished woman's grave on Bäckerstrasse, 6th century (Swiss National Museum, Zurich).

Settlement continued continuously in Roman times. Contrary to earlier views, the stationing of Roman military did not occur only during the Alpine campaign 16-15 BC, but already from 40 or 30 BC in the existing Celtic settlement. This is indicated by finds of military equipment and imported goods from the Mediterranean region such as thin-walled ceramics, sigillata tableware and oil lamps with pictorial motifs. On both sides of the Limmat, a civilian small-town center (vicus?) developed. A gravestone dated around 200 names the Statio Turicensis, a customs station of the Gallic customs for trade in the border area to Rhaetia. A public bath stood at the bay under Weinplatz. A harbor and river crossing are suspected near Rathausbrücke. On the Grosse Hafner, a former island in front of Seefeld, there was an island sanctuary used from the 1st to 4th centuries, which according to dendrochronology was newly built in 122 on a round plan with wooden posts. Another temple possibly existed in the round building uncovered at Storchengasse. The dedicatory stone donated by bear hunters (ursari) to the deities Diana and Silvanus and a hoard of gold jewelry possibly indicate another sanctuary in the Oetenbach area. A fragment of a four-god stone comes from the base of a Jupiter giant statue. On the archaeologically investigated residential buildings, the transition to stone construction can be observed around 70.

In late Roman times, probably in the early 4th century, the summit of the Lindenhof hill was fortified with a castellum, which offered residence and refuge to the civilian population even after the withdrawal of the troops and the end of Western Roman administration. The burials examined in the Bäckerstrasse cemetery from the 6th century suggest a majority Roman-speaking population. Among them is a woman's grave with a Germanic fibula costume pointing towards the Frankish area. The plate and wall graves investigated on St. Petershügel were built using mortar, plaster and lime whitewash. They prove that building techniques introduced in Roman times were used in a 7th-century cemetery. The grave goods of two swords (spatha, sax) in a male grave follow Germanic burial customs. Within the castellum, several stone buildings were erected in the 7th and 8th centuries after terrain works. Remains of wooden houses from the same time were found in Niederdorf.
City of kings and dukes (8th to 12th century)

In the 8th and 9th centuries, Zurich was the center of an extensive Carolingian imperial estate complex of political and economic importance. With the fiscus Zurich created around 760, an administrative organization emerged that referred to functions of the old castellum site. This included the royal court, which among other things included the Albis forest and properties in Uri and whose economic center was the Stadelhof. Ludwig the German equipped the Fraumünster monastery with this in a deed of donation in 853. Abbesses were his daughters Hildegard and Berta, demonstrating the close connection of the convent to the royal house. Foundations of a monumental building uncovered on Lindenhof are interpreted as remains of a Carolingian palace building. For the dukes of Swabia appointed in the 10th century as bailiffs for the secular and ecclesiastical royal property, Zurich was a center of their rule. Coin minting, market and toll rights illustrate the importance of economy and trade. In the 11th and 12th centuries, economic relations up to the Baltic Sea area are documented.

After 1000, royal visits to Zurich resumed: Henry III stayed six times in the palace on Lindenhof between 1045-1055 and had it expanded into a residence with a two-story hall and chapel. After losing the function as a palace, Otto of Freising in the mid-12th century still described Zurich as the most distinguished city of Swabia. In the Staufer-Zähringer compromise of 1098, Zurich left the domain of the Staufer dukes. The counts of Lenzburg, who were already appointed as provosts and monastery bailiffs in 976, were confirmed, and the dukes of Zähringen were appointed holders of imperial rights. After the extinction of the Lenzburg line, the Zähringers were the sole city lords from 1173 to 1218. The conversion of the royal palace into a castle with towers and ditches is probably attributed to them.

The Fraumünster and Grossmünster convents formed in the 10th century, together with the Wasserkirche and the parish churches of St. Peter and St. Stephan, an exceptional sacred landscape shaped by the local martyr cult of Felix and Regula. The oldest archaeologically proven church of the Benedictine nunnery Fraumünster is a large hall church of the 9th century with a transept and three apses. Before it stood an early medieval post building of unknown function. In its early period, the monastery had an enclosure with a ditch. The collegiate church Grossmünster was regarded as the place of burial of the city saints. The passion story written down at the end of the 8th century reports miracles at their graves, suggesting that a cult building already existed at that time. It is unknown whether Charlemagne, revered as the founder, had sought after the burial site. The Grossmünster church was rebuilt in late Romanesque style between 1100 and 1230, replacing a predecessor building. The Wasserkirche, whose oldest predecessor can be dated to 1000, houses the martyr's stone. This indicated the spot on a Limmat island that was venerated as the place of the beheading of the city saints. The church of St. Peter, first mentioned in 857, is attested as a parish church from the 12th century; it possibly followed on the vanished church of St. Stephan west of Lindenhof. Due to a donation, the Augustinian canons' monastery of St. Martin was founded on Zurichberg in 1127.

Written sources from the 8th century provide clues about the settlement's topography: castrum, castellum and civitas refer to the castellum or castle site; vicus to the unfortified settlement parts; villa and curtis to the farmsteads. From Carolingian times come wooden buildings near Fraumünster and embankments for a probable embankment at the eastern Limmat bank. The expanded defensive ditch of Lindenhof at upper Rennweg is dated to the 10th-11th century. The intensive building activity of the 12th century was also recorded in written sources. Archaeologically, the first extensive city wall and a bossed square stone wall on the Limmat shore are evidenced. In the eastern city district, regular sequences of building complexes, alleys and moats give the impression of planned plots. The four-story core building of the Guild House of the Carpenters is dendro-dated to 1156.
Rule and politics from the High Middle Ages to the end of the 18th century
The city becomes independent

The imperial bailiwick Zurich, assigned in 1098 to the Dukes of Zähringen, continued after their extinction in 1218 but was no longer granted by the king as a hereditary office to a prince, rather limited in time to an imperial official, usually coming from the citizenry. The imperial immediacy of the city, certified several times until 1512 by emperor and empire, formed the basis for the gradual development of municipal self-government. The old center of power on Lindenhof must have been destroyed by citizens in the early 13th century, long before 1271 according to written records.

Like the Grossmünster chapter, the Fraumünster chapter was freed from bailiff interference. Its abbess attained the rank of imperial princess (attested from 1234), appointed the mayor early on, and influenced the election of other officials. She granted the coin and toll rights, determined minting standards and measures, and long also certified municipal legal transactions with her seal. From the late 13th century, the manorial rights and prerogatives of the abbey increasingly came under the influence of the economically empowered bourgeoisie, for example in the form of fixed-term grants of coinage rights (similar to market or toll rights). However, lower jurisdiction remained with the convent. The abbess also certified the "Sworn Letters" and law books until Emperor Sigismund allowed the citizenry in 1433 to change legal texts independently. Due to the economic decline of Fraumünster, the city increasingly intervened in monastery affairs in the late Middle Ages. Although economic conditions improved, the monastery was dissolved in the Reformation in 1524 and its property confiscated. The city combined the Fraumünster estate into the Fraumünster office. The former monastery's assets were administered separately from the other monastic holdings, and the office of Obmann established in 1533 to manage it.
Municipal constitution and city institutions
Oldest seal stamp of the city of Zurich, 1347 (State Archives Zurich, OBJ 19).

A council is attested in Zurich from 1220. Since the imperial bailiff presided over the council, it is assumed that it evolved from the imperial bailiff's court. Until the mid-13th century, the exact competences of the council are not known, but its members initially mainly appeared as witnesses in property transfers. From 1250, it is better traceable through council lists (fully mentioned in 1252). The council of twelve members, consisting of knights and citizens, divided itself into fasten (Lent), summer, and autumn councils, each with a term of four months. This document was issued in the town hall mentioned first in 1252 (in domo nostrae universitatis). The judge's letter first drafted around 1250 is the oldest codification of the city's laws. In the renewed version of 1304, the formation of guilds as political groups was forbidden, but they remained as trade guilds.

After the failed attack on Winterthur in 1292, the bourgeois-commercial patriciate increasingly displaced the knights from the council. The rise of the patricians was halted in 1336 by the Brun guild revolution. In the "First Sworn Letter," the council is divided into a Baptistal and Natal council with six-month terms each. It consisted of 26 members: 13 members were from the Konstaffel, which comprised seven knights and six major merchants (consules), and the other 13 were guild masters (scabini) of the 13 newly formed guilds. Mayor Rudolf Brun was elected for life with dictatorial powers. The councilors banished to Rapperswil unsuccessfully tried to regain power, including in the Zurich murder night of 1350. The guild constitution remained in a modified form until 1798.
Initial of the "Second Sworn Letter," 1373 (State Archives Zurich, C I, Nr. 536).

In the "Second Sworn Letter" of 1373, the mayor’s powers were curtailed in favor of the council and his term restricted to the six-month council cycle. The councilors of the Konstaffel should now be elected by the outgoing council, the consules and scabini, leading to an increase of merchants and landowners in the council at the expense of knights. The craftsmen became eligible for the council, whereas previously they were only represented via the guild masters. The "Third Sworn Letter" agreed in 1393 after the so-called Schöno treaty sanctioned the election of guild members among the consules and made the Great Council together with the Small Council the supreme state authority. After the pogroms against Jews in 1401, the Great Council not only defended its right to self-appointment but also effectively elected the guild superiors. From the 15th century, the guild masters' college took control over council and guilds based on guaranteed rights. After Hans Waldmann's overthrow in 1489 (Waldmannhandel), guild powers were again limited to trade rights. According to the "Fourth" or "Fifth Sworn Letter" of 1498, professional groups such as merchants, goldsmiths, landowners, and free trades had free guild choice, breaking through the guild constitution, concentrating power in the hands of an upper class at the expense of craftsmen, and further weakening the Konstaffel. From 1490, Hintersassen (dependent residents) and thus part of the poorer population were also included in the Konstaffel.

The Great Council or Council of Two Hundred consisted from the late 15th century of both mayors, 48 members of the old and new Small Councils, 144 Zwölfer (12 councilors from each of the twelve guilds), and the Achtzehner (18 Konstaffel members), totaling 212 members. The small councils were elected by the sitting small and great councilors. The Great Council's competences included decisions on war and peace, conclusion of new alliances, election of mayor, council, bailiffs, and officials, as well as tax matters. Important transactions were submitted to the Secret Council, initially differently composed and eventually formed by the nine bodily heads, for prior consultation; this college was permanently established from 1633. Other important bodies were the accounting council responsible for the state budget and the war council.

Until the end of the Ancien Régime, the "Sworn Letters" were amended twice more. The "Sixth Sworn Letter" of 1654 confirmed the free guild choice of merchants, consolidating their supremacy. The "Seventh Sworn Letter," enacted in response to the civil unrest of 1712-1713, did not change this situation. Thus, the share of merchants in the citizenry rose from 3% in 1599 to 12% in 1790, their presence in the council rising from 8% to 40%. To impede office buying (praktizieren), secret elections of guild masters were introduced, though they did not prevent re-election. As authority prevailed over craftsmen, this last constitutional reform stalled in its approach, but internal conflicts within the ruling elite diminished.

Already from the late 15th century, in Zurich—similar to other guild cities—aristocratization and intensification of absolutist state developed, favored by the strengthened closure of citizenship rights from mid-16th century and the prospect of gaining bailiff and monastery offices due to Reformation and secularization. Political careers became attractive, with wealth and personal networks decisive for elections. The city's acquisition of church tasks led to expansion of the administrative apparatus, mainly in social, educational, and health services, while police-military functions like general service duties and guard service partly remained with the Konstaffel and guilds. By the late 18th century, the guilds as corporations mainly had organizational roles; political authority was led by the elite of merchants and city nobility. The citizenry's competences during the Ancien Régime were limited to the convening citizen assembly as needed and taking the citizen oath on the pledge days.
City layout, public and private buildings

On the right bank of the Limmat, the so-called "More City" developed with the watch posts Auf Dorf, Linden, Neumarkt, and Niederdorf; on the left bank, the "Lesser City" with the watch posts Münsterhof and Rennweg. Outside the city center, the three suburb quarters Hirschengraben, Stadelhofen, and Talacker arose. The walled city covered 38 hectares and was separated from the surroundings by outlying defensive walls. With the building of fortifications in the 13th century, which followed an older city wall, the political center shifted from Lindenhof to the Limmat. In this related city expansion, the Oetenbach monastery and Rennweg on the left of the Limmat were established. The two parts of the city were connected by two bridges, which arose in the first half of the 13th century: the lower or Rathausbrücke and the upper or Münsterbrücke. Two bridges also crossed the Sihl. Mills stood on the Mühlestege, on the right Limmat bank and further downstream. For defensive, urban planning, and economic reasons, a star-shaped fortification was built from 1642 to the 18th century, doubling the walled area.
City view from the north, 1770. Copper engraving from the series Hundert Schweizer-Prospecte by Johann Balthasar Bullinger (Central Library Zurich, Department Maps and Panoramas).

Sacred buildings, stone houses such as knight towers and guild houses, and wooden buildings shaped the late medieval cityscape. Closed alleys emerged from the 14th and 15th centuries. Early stone buildings grouped around the church centers Fraumünster, Grossmünster, St. Peter, and the two Limmat bridges. For grain trade, the Kornhaus at Weinplatz was set up in the late 13th century, but relocated to the upper bridge in the 17th century. After a first town hall, a second was built from 1397 at the same place, and from 1694-1698 the still existing building on the right Limmat bank. Also on the Limmat, the courthouse (later main guard) was built around 1468, the Helmhaus mentioned in 1253 on the gable side of the Wasserkirche, serving textile trade, quality and measure control, and goods toll collection, and opposite it, the Hottinger tower with Kaufhaus from 1412 and later salt house. The building office was responsible for public construction projects. Besides the shooting house on the square northwest of the medieval city walls, the Bauhaus in the Kratz quarter was the most important representative building of the 16th century.

After the expulsion of the Jewish community in 1436, the synagogue at Froschaugasse was integrated into a residential building. Monasteries and city churches dissolved in the Reformation were repurposed. For example, the Holy Spirit hospital in Niederdorf took over the buildings of the Prediger monastery, and the secularized Wasserkirche was converted into a citizen library with art chamber from 1633 to 1639. Important secular buildings from the 17th and 18th centuries include extended or newly built guild houses and houses Zur Krone (later Rechberg), Zum Florhof, and Zum Kiel, as well as outside the fortifications the Freigut, the Muralt estate in Enge, and the Beckenhof in Unterstrass.
Society, economy, and culture from the High Middle Ages to the end of the 18th century
Economy

In the late Middle Ages, the silk trade, documented from the 13th century, flourished in Zurich and was at the center of extensive trading relations. This also benefited wool and linen weavers as well as the leather industry. Long-distance trade required the presence of Jewish, Lombard, and southern French moneylenders, who left traces in frescoes in the house at Brunnenhof or the "Lamparterturm" at the upper fences. After the Brun's revolt in 1336 and the plague year of 1350, textile trades and long-distance trade declined. After the Old Zurich War, the silk trade collapsed. Zurich retained a regional market for daily goods as well as grain, wine, salt, and iron trade. Long-distance trade was conducted via Gotthard and Graubünden passes.

Coat of arms of the South German Counts of Helfenstein. Detail from the coat of arms frieze in the painted festival hall of Jewish banker Mordechai ben Menachem in the house at Brunnenhof, around 1330 (Photography City Archaeology Zurich).

Until the end of the Ancien Régime, Zurich was a guild city shaped by the guild constitution. The city held the market monopoly and protected the activities of the city's craftsmen against external competition. Innovations were only possible outside the guild-regulated areas. Attempts at export-oriented economic activities were immediately monopolized in favor of the corporative interests of the guild oligarchy-dominated city merchants. Of the once significant textile trade, in the first half of the 16th century only cloth production had supra-regional importance. From the mid-century, Protestant refugees gave new impetus to the textile industry. Thanks to their trade relations with Italy, the silk industry returned to Zurich, but many newly founded weaving companies succumbed to guild pressure. From 1620, the number of textile publishers clearly increased with some fluctuations. Merchant-publishers, emerging from the citizenry and Huguenots who arrived in Zurich and developed their activities outside guild constraints, prevailed over the guild-organized textile industry. To defend their interests, they formed the Commercial Directorate in 1662 (dissolved in 1834). Textile manufacturers specialized as Marchand-Banquiers and opened private banks. The state-owned Interest Commission founded in 1755, which later became Bank Leu, also functioned as a bank. However, as a financial and trading center, Zurich lagged behind Basel, Geneva, and St. Gallen until the mid-19th century.
Society

Between the 9th and 12th centuries, three social groups are recognizable among Zurich's lay population: unfree persons of the monastery and chapter, so-called church dependents; unfree persons of the palace and royal property, called fiscalians; and the people of Zurichberg (homines de monte), probably free. In the first half of the 12th century, this differentiation disappeared in favor of uniform designations for city inhabitants: laici de loco, cives, concives, burgenses, urbani. These consisted of citizens, residents and dependent residents. In the late Middle Ages, knights and bourgeois patriciate formed the upper class, most craftsmen the middle class, and penniless craftsmen, journeymen, and many single women the lower class. Social mobility between classes was possible. A certain social gradient from center to periphery near the city walls, such as in Kratz quarter, can be observed.

The citizenry divided into social and occupational groups: landowners, magistrates, traders, merchants, craftsmen, free professions and clerics. Landowners lived as nobles from their assets or held high public offices. Together with traders and merchants, they were the politically dominant force, while craftsmen's influence declined in early modern times. Among merchants, iron, salt, and textile merchants were initially at the top, later export-oriented merchants, textile publishers, and bankers. From 1409, all citizens belonged to a guild or the Konstaffel; free professions such as lawyers, doctors and teachers could be admitted to a guild or the Konstaffel by election. Parish posts in Zurich's surroundings, except for some Winterthur collations, were reserved for citizens and offered advancement opportunities for craftsmen's sons. Residents, including maids, other servants, and journeymen, had limited duration in the city; the Hintersassen deployed mainly in non-guild trades and proto-industrial subcontracting were granted city admission depending on economic needs. Their share of the city population remained relatively low.

The guilds exercised social and cultural functions alongside political and economic roles. Public life was regulated by ethics mandates. From the late medieval guild kitchen meal developed in the 18th century the Sechseläuten festival, marking the start of spring. First parades took place from 1818. The Boy Shooting, dating back to the Thirty Years' War, was institutionalized only in 1809.
Church and religious life

In the late Middle Ages, diverse religious life prevailed, with the cult of Felix and Regula playing a central identity-shaping role. Churches and monasteries were of great importance for city development and generously endowed like the hospital and leper houses St. Jakob and Spanweid. In the 13th century, the women's monasteries Oetenbach, St. Verena, and Selnau were founded, as well as mendicant order monasteries of Augustinian hermits, Franciscans, and preachers. Beguines and Beghards were settled near the mendicant orders.

During the Reformation, monasteries were dissolved, and monastic properties transferred to city ownership. The post-Reformation Grossmünster chapter took on new tasks, especially in theology education. In 1525, a civil-ecclesiastical marriage court was introduced. The Antistes, also first pastor at Grossmünster, was elected for life by the council. As head of the Zurich church, he presided over the church-political examiners' convention and the church synod. In the 17th century, a dogmatic church dominated city public life. The shift from Protestant orthodoxy to Enlightenment rationalism and Pietism was not without resistance. In 1685, a French church was established for Protestant refugees. Catholic mass was celebrated again for the first time only in 1799.
Education and culture

The first city schools were Latin schools at Fraumünster and Grossmünster. German schools taught basic knowledge in reading, writing, and arithmetic, initially for boys only. After the Reformation, the church reorganized the school system together with city government. The highest level was the Prophezei (from the 17th century Carolinum), founded by Huldrych Zwingli, which trained theologians and later also offered natural science and history subjects. An intermediate level was the Collegium humanitatis. For university education, young Zurichers mainly went to Protestant universities of the empire. Based on Enlightenment ideas, new school types emerged: in 1774 the art school and in 1782 the medical-surgical institute were opened. From 1645, the citizens' library published New Year's leaflets for educating Zurich youth; the first newspapers appeared from the first half of the 17th century. In the same century, first societies emerged, among them the Collegium Insulanum founded in 1679 and the Collegium anatomicum of 1685; in the 18th century, among others the physical society founded in 1746 and the mathematical-military society founded in 1765.

Music life in Zurich mainly took place in the domestic sphere, church, and various music societies like the 1613-founded Society at the Music Hall. In the 16th century, plays were performed on Münsterhof, involving the whole city. Theater life ceased completely in 1624 under Antistes Johann Jakob Breitinger (1575-1645) due to puritan rigorism. Thanks to Johann Jakob Bodmer and Johann Jakob Breitinger (1701-1776), Zurich became a center of German-language literature in the 18th century. Prominent artists and academics included Johann Heinrich Füssli, Salomon Gessner, Johann Kaspar Lavater, and Johann Heinrich Rahn.
Political-administrative development in the 19th and 20th centuries
Municipal constitution and authorities

After the Helvetic Revolution of 1798, the Helvetic unitary state and its cantonal administrative units succeeded the old city-state legal system. The political municipality of active resident citizens, led by the municipality, was joined by the citizen community in 1799. This was directed by the community chamber and took on poor relief and management of municipal properties. In the Mediation period, the community assembly of citizens and residents with a two-year residence or city real estate ownership elected a 15-member city council according to the cantonal municipality law of 1803. In 1816, the cantonal Great Council enacted an organizational law for the city council based on the Restoration Constitution. The latter was assigned the Larger City Council, which consisted of five representatives from each of the 13 cantonal-city election guilds. This committee elected the municipal council, city president, and peaceful judges. It also decided on citizenship rights and city land transactions. The Regeneration Constitution of 1831 granted municipalities the right to enact own municipal regulations. According to the first Zurich municipality ordinance of 1831, there was a Small City Council of seven members alongside the community assembly as highest organ, and a 60-member Large City Council. The latter was elected until 1866 by the election guilds, although these had already been abolished at cantonal level in 1838. In 1875, based on superior laws, the poor and citizen community existing since 1803 as a territorial corporation was abolished and converted into a personal association of city citizens living in Zurich. In 1881, Small and Large City Councils were separated personnel-wise. They have since been elected at ballot box. The cantonal allocation law abolished the community assembly in 1891 and introduced the municipal initiative and referendum. The municipality ordinance of 1892 increased the number of city councilors from seven to nine. Since 1913, the Large City Council has been elected proportionally. The 1933 municipality ordinance renamed the parliament to municipal council. Municipal women's suffrage was introduced in 1969. From the last total revision of the municipality ordinance from 1970 until 2010, 44 partial revisions took place.
The municipal area

In 1798, the city was divided into three sections: Oberdorf, Niederdorf, and Kleine Stadt. The strong immigration in the 19th century, which mainly affected suburbs and financially overwhelmed them, ultimately led to the first incorporation of 1893, prompted by the Aussersihl petition of 1885. It made Zurich the largest Swiss city. The 1891 cantonal allocation law fixed the division into five Zurich districts then still numbered with Roman numerals: Altstadt (I), Enge, Leimbach and Wollishofen (II), Aussersihl and Wiedikon (III), Oberstrass, Unterstrass and Wipkingen (IV), and Fluntern, Hirslanden, Hottingen and Riesbach (V). In 1913, these were increased to eight. The 1933 municipality ordinance before the second incorporation of 1934 divided Zurich into eleven precincts: Altstadt (1), Enge, Leimbach and Wollishofen (2), Wiedikon (3), Aussersihl (4), Industriequartier (5), Oberstrass and Unterstrass (6), Fluntern, Hirslanden, Hottingen and Witikon (7), Riesbach (8), Albisrieden and Altstetten (9), Höngg and Wipkingen (10), and Affoltern, Oerlikon, Schwamendingen and Seebach (11). Since 1970, Schwamendingen forms district 12.
