Political forces

From 1799 to mid-19th century, conservatives dominated city politics. Urban liberals played a mainly cantonal role from 1830. After their return to power in the canton, they began to dominate city politics after 1845. In the 1860s, conservatives arranged with liberals and joined them politically. Strong immigration from mid-19th century favored the rise of the democratic movement anchored mainly in Winterthur and rural areas, also advocating social reform. In 1866, the first non-citizen, tinsmith Jakob Schnurrenberger, was elected to the Small City Council. Until the first incorporation, Zurich was a liberal stronghold. The last bastion of conservative-minded urban citizens, the citizen community, fell with the municipality law of 1875, which made naturalization of Swiss citizens easier. Democrats became the strongest force in the suburbs.
Poster of the Free Democratic Party for city and municipal council elections in 1928, designed by ad agency Max Dalang (Swiss Social Archive, Zurich, F Ob-0003-022).
Election poster of the Social Democratic Party of the city of Zurich, designed by Otto Baumberger, 1931 (Museum of Design Zurich, Poster Collection, Zurich University of the Arts).

In the Large City Council or Municipal Council, the liberal party (from 1917 FDP) dominated until 1907, then the SP took over. From 1928-1938, "red Zurich" had an absolute parliamentary majority. In 1938, the National Ring of Independents (LdU) entered the municipal council. Together with the CVP, which founded a city party section as Christian Social Party in 1907, and the Evangelical People's Party, the political center was formed until the late 1970s. In 2002, the SVP, emerging from the Farmers, Trades, and Citizens Party, replaced the FDP as the strongest bourgeois force.

In the executive city council, the democratic party dominated from 1892-1901 with five of nine seats, from 1907 the SP with four, and from 1928 with five seats. "Red Zurich" ended in 1949 with the death of city president Adolf Lüchinger. From 1950, the SP generally held four seats, the FDP and the dissolved LdU each one to two. In 1970, Emilie Lieberherr (SP) became the first woman elected to the city council. In 1990, the SP became strongest party again, while the SVP exited. Since 1994, a red-green majority has governed.
City assets and finances

The assets of the former city-state passed to the Helvetic Republic, which provisionally left properties to the city in 1798. The 1803 mediation act secured assets covering costs for school, poor relief, church, and construction. Police were financed by fees and consumption taxes. From 1802, the city charged billeting fees per household. From 1833, residents were taxed for police, school, church, and road construction. Those owning property paid contributions for public buildings and fire brigade. The 1855 municipality law equated residents and citizens tax-wise; direct municipal taxes were introduced but did not yet affect poor relief. The 1891 allocation law introduced a modern municipal tax system.
Social welfare

Until 1835, church communities were responsible for poor relief; then city central poor authority and general poor support fund were established. Private charity, e.g., the Relief Society or Community Society, remained necessary complement well into the 20th century. The city gradually expanded social benefits. Before the domicile principle replaced the hometown principle in social assistance, rising mobility in 19th century made the association-organized and municipality-supported "Voluntary and Resident Poor Relief of the City of Zurich" (1878-1929) necessary. Since 1907, the city directly or indirectly supports housing construction via cooperative support.
City utilities and enterprises

The street lighting introduced privately in 1778 became a public task in 1855. To this end, a gasworks was built, initially as a concession company, and operated by the municipality from 1886. It was located at Platzspitz until 1867, then in Industriequartier and from 1898 in Schlieren. Conversion to natural gas happened in 1974.
Construction of Zurich water supply pipelines at Schanzengraben near the Botanical Garden of the University. Photograph by Eduard Schucht, 1885 (Building History Archive of the City of Zurich).
Sewer reform 1867. Sample plan of municipal engineering office for homeowners, 1867 (City Archive Zurich, Planning Archive).

After the cholera epidemic of 1855, criticism of hygienic conditions in waste disposal arose. From 1860-1873, the sewage system was built; the sewer reform followed in 1867. In 1868, drinking water supply was improved to provide public fountains with spring water and households with process water from the Limmat. After a typhus epidemic in 1884, water was taken from the lake and since 1895 also spring water from the Sihl and Lorze valleys. In 1904, the waste incineration plant opened; in 1923, the construction of the sewage treatment plant and combined sewer system was decided. The municipal Letten power plant began operation in 1892. The city strongly engaged in hydropower plants (Albula, Heidsee, Limmat Wettingen, Julia Tiefencastel, Julia Marmorera, Bergell power plants) or participated in water and nuclear power plants (Maggia, Blenio, Hinterrhein as well as the nuclear plants Gösgen and Leibstadt, Bugey and Cattenom in France). The private "Rösslitram" opened in 1888 was municipalized in 1894 and electrified in 1900. By 1931, the Municipal Tramway Zurich (VBZ from 1950) took over all private tram companies. The Zurich Transport Network, the merger of VBZ with seven other transport companies, began operation together with the S-Bahn in 1990.
Society, economy, and culture in the 19th and 20th centuries
Urban development and transportation

Until 1830, only the core city was densely built; the rest of the city area consisted of meadows, fields, vineyards, forest, isolated farms and villas of city dwellers. From 1780, deconstruction of the medieval city wall began. From 1833, the canton started demolishing fortifications, creating space for public buildings and roads. With the construction of Münster bridge and Limmatquai from 1835, Zurich oriented itself from the Limmat towards the lake. The station outside the old town opened in 1847, sparking a large construction phase from 1860 to 1890. By 1859, the Limmatquai was built; from 1861-1863, the Bahnhofbrücke; 1864-1869 the Zeughaus; 1873-1875 a barracks in Aussersihl; from 1864, Bahnhofstrasse; from 1867 the Bahnhof district; 1861-1864 the Polytechnical School; 1865-1871 the new main train station; and 1873-1875 the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt at Paradeplatz. Zurich expanded its city boundary into Selnau and at Neumühlequai and laid out the Fraumünster district from 1875, the Prediger district from 1876-1878, and the Industriequartier in Aussersihl from 1877-1880. From 1880-1890, the stock exchange and upper Bahnhofstrasse, lake promenade and Quaibrücke were built, followed by construction of the lakeside and Stadthausquai. The new administrative center planned by Gustav Gull with office buildings on the Oetenbach site and along Schipfe, as well as a street connection from Zähringerplatz to Rämistrasse, was only partially realized. The structure of the main road network goes back to the general development plan of 1899. The international competition for a development plan for Zurich and its suburbs (1915-1918) strongly shaped future development.
Urban development of Zurich 1850-2000
Development of the Zurich agglomeration since 1930

From 1930, the city acquired houses for old town renovation. In 1962, the old town was placed under city protection, often leading to hollowing out of old town houses. The concept of a car-friendly city was only partially realized, including widening Bahnhof- and Limmatquai, Bahnhof bridge, and Central. However, the high-performance road around the old town, planned in the 1955 general traffic plan, a rejected underground or deep tram in the 1962 referendum, and an underground railway rejected in 1973, were not built. The city tried to solve inner-city traffic problems with federal funds by promoting highway construction, but the opening of the provisional western tangent in 1972 led to a rethink. Environmental concerns regularly found political majorities. The deindustrialization from the 1970s caused a financial crisis in the 1990s but also created free spaces, enabling the boom in Zurich-West and repurposing of industrial areas into service and residential districts in Oerlikon, Giesshübel, Binz, Altstetten, and Affoltern.
Economy

At the beginning of the 19th century, cotton and silk industries dominated city economy. In 1805, the mechanical cotton spinning mill, later Escher Wyss & Cie. machine factory, was founded at Neumühlequai. Mills on the Limmat were converted into textile factories by 1895. Silk trade and processing took place in Zurich, weaving was located outside the city. Construction of the railway from 1847 enabled Zurich's development as an industrial center and transport hub. With Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, created in 1856 to finance the textile industry and railway construction, Zurich became a banking center. Schweizerische Rentenanstalt (1857) and Schweizerische Rückversicherungsanstalt (1863) founded the insurance sector in Zurich. Towards the end of the 19th century, heavy industry shifted from the center to outskirts in Aussersihl and Oerlikon. By 1930, the textile industry lost its leading role to metal, machinery and electrical industries. In the same period, Zurich rose to Switzerland's financial center: In 1929, a quarter of all bank employees and a third of all insurance employees in Switzerland worked in Zurich. In the 1980s and 1990s, financial institutions outsourced parts of their jobs to suburbs, and the Zurich region became one of the world's ten largest financial centers. In the second half of the 20th century, the city also became Switzerland's media center. Apart from major Zurich newspapers "Neue Zürcher Zeitung" and "Tages-Anzeiger," tabloid and popular press such as Blick were published here. Also, German- and Romansh-speaking Swiss television settled in Zurich.
Social structure and social change

In the early 19th century, politically and economically, the minority of old Zurich families who had belonged to the regime before 1798 dominated. They long distinguished themselves from the advancing bourgeoisie until distinctions began to blur in the late 19th century. This upper class met in partly exclusive clubs such as Schildner zum Schneggen, Bogenschützen (archers), the old Zurich club "zur weißen Rose", or Reitclub Zurich. More middle-class oriented were the guilds and some cultural and sports associations such as the Hottingen reading circle or the Grasshopper Club. Craftsmen made up the majority of city population until equality of city and countryside, abolition of privileges by ending the guild system in 1837, and industrialization undermined their economic basis.
Population development of the city of Zurich 1836-2010

Industrialization and immigration radically changed the population structure. The share of citizens in the city population was still 55.9% around 1800. By 1836, residents had the majority. Immigration from Inner and Eastern Switzerland, southern Germany, Austria, later from Italy and other Mediterranean countries, turned Zurich, which was purely Reformed until 1798, into a mixed-denomination city. The composition of nationalities changed radically as well. Germans arrived from about 1830 as academics or skilled workers, some as political refugees to Zurich, where they founded a support association in 1856. Around 1900, immigrant workers from Germany were mostly female. Italians immigrated from the 1880s mainly from northern rural Italy, were mainly employed in construction and gradually organized in workers' associations.

Economic and demographic upheavals also caused social tensions that erupted in 1871 in the Tonhalle riots and 1896 in the Italian riots. Already before, social conflicts manifested despite the cantonal ban on trade unions from 1844-1869 in first strikes by shoemakers, tinsmiths, locksmiths, carpenters, and stonemasons, reaching a first peak in 1870. More than 50 strikes took place in Zurich in 1906-1907. The painters' and locksmiths' strike led in 1912 to the general strike. The worsening living conditions in World War I radicalized workers and fostered revolutionary and pacifist ideas culminating in the November riots of 1917 and the national strike of 1918. From 1914, the number of foreigners decreased continuously until after World War II, although Zurich especially from 1933 was a destination for political and artistic refugees from Germany.

The economic upswing after World War II largely dissolved social milieus, which had lived through dense networks of clubs, meeting places, newspapers and publishers, sports clubs and festivals. They were replaced by lifestyles. In social topography, the Zurichberg-Aussersihl/Industriequartier contrast was increasingly replaced by center-periphery contrast. From 1950, a second Italian labor immigration began; in the 1970s, this was replaced by migration from further Mediterranean countries. A renewed significant influx of immigrants from EU states, especially Germany, started after Switzerland concluded bilateral agreements with the EU in 2002.
Churches and religious life

Until 1798, only Reformed lived in Zurich, divided into four church parishes Grossmünster, Fraumünster, St. Peter and Prediger. In 2013, there were 34. The first of today's 23 Catholic parishes emerged in 1807. The parish church was initially the St. Anna Chapel, from 1833 the Fraumünster, and from 1842-1873 the Augustiner church, which during the culture struggle was given to the newly formed Christian Catholic community. In 1874, St. Peter and Paul in Aussersihl was consecrated.

Before permanent settlement freedom was granted in 1862, Jews, mainly from Endingen, Lengnau (AG), southern Germany and Alsace, were only tolerated. In the same year, some of these immigrants, including members of the Ris family, founded the Israelite Cultus Community. Eastern European immigration began in the 1870s. The Israelite Religious Community formed in 1895, Agudas Achim in 1912 and Or Chadasch in 1978. Altogether, Jewish communities never had substantially more than 6,000 members. Anti-Semitic prejudices against poor East European Jewish immigrants led in 1910 to extended residence requirements and in 1920 to a criterion aimed especially at Orthodox Jews of adequate assimilation in naturalizations. In 1963, the first mosque in Switzerland, the Mahmoud Mosque, was opened in Zurich. The growth of Muslims of various faiths mainly stems from immigration of laborers and political refugees from former Yugoslavia and Turkey.
Education

From 1831-1833, liberals comprehensively reformed the cantonal school system and integrated the existing city educational institutions into the new system. The university opened in 1833, allowing women to study from 1840, and the Polytechnic (Federal Institutes of Technology) founded in 1855 were strongly influenced by professors from neighboring countries in the 19th century and gave impulses to the city’s cultural life. They produced some Nobel Prize winners and made Zurich a research site. Private associations such as the Antiquarian Society founded in 1832, the Museum Society founded in 1834 and the Scholars Society founded in 1837, were important research and educational institutions until the 20th century. In 1976, the city’s Higher Daughters’ School (founded in 1875) was transferred to the canton; in 1988, the canton took over the vocational school (founded in 1873) and the School of Applied Arts (founded in 1878). The latter was transformed into the School of Design and Art in 1998 and integrated into the University of the Arts in 2007.
Music, theater and visual arts – festivals and performances

While music life flourished in the 18th and 19th centuries—the three music societies merged in 1812 into the General Music Society—church circles prevented theater until the 1830s. In 1834, the speech and music stage of the Aktie Theater was established, directed by Charlotte Birch-Pfeiffer from 1837-1843, lasting until 1890. Richard Wagner also gave concerts at the casino on Hirschengraben (1806-1874). The Tonhalle in the Kornhaus at Bellevue opened provisionally in 1867 for the Swiss Music Festival and definitely with the founding of the Tonhalle Society a year later. The director of the Tonhalle Orchestra, Friedrich Hegar, was also co-initiator of the Zurich Music School (from 1907 Conservatory) founded in 1876. After the Aktie Theater burned down, the city theater at Bellevue was built in 1891, renamed Opera House in 1964. The new Tonhalle built in 1895 replaced the Tonhalle in the Kornhaus demolished in 1897; in 1937, it was integrated into the Congress House. Director Ferdinand Rieser turned the Volkstheater at Pfauen founded in 1892 into the Schauspielhaus, which from 1933 became the most important independent stage in the German-speaking world. The Neue Schauspiel AG, founded in 1938, also plays the Schiffbauhalle in Zurich-West since 2000.

On the initiative of the Art Society, which itself emerged from the Zurich Artists' Society founded in 1787, the Kunsthaus was founded in 1910. It gained international importance only after World War II thanks to numerous donations. In the second half of the 20th century, important collections came to Zurich, such as Baron Eduard von der Heydt's collection of non-European art in the city Museum Rietberg opened in 1952, the collection of the Migros cooperative federation in the Museum of Contemporary Art opened in 1996 in Löwenbräu area, or the collection of the foundation for constructive and concrete art founded in 1986 in Haus Konstruktiv (EWZ substation Selnau) opened in 2001. They brought Zurich into focus of leading international art galleries.

Besides traditional festivals Sechseläuten and Knabenschiessen, several national singing, gymnastic and shooting festivals took place in Zurich, the national exhibitions of 1883 and 1939, and the Saffa in 1958. The Dada movement was founded in Zurich in 1916. Since 1936, June Festival Weeks (from 1997 Zurich Festival), since 1951 the Zurich Fest, since 1980 the Zurich Theater Spectacle, since 1991 the Street Parade, and since 2005 the Zurich Film Festival have been held.
